It was suggested that individual members of the commission would be under the cabinet's thumb. I think I explained at the time that the purpose of the

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for the further explanation he has given of this bill the principle of which, as he says, was discussed at considerable length when the resolution was before the house. It is not my intention to make prolonged remarks with regard to this bill. As I say, the principle of the bill was discussed on March 4 at the resolution stage and we will have an opportunity to discuss it in the committee which has been set up to deal with veterans matters.
At the hearings of that committee we will have an opportunity to hear representatives of the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations with regard to different sections of the bill. We shall also have before us officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs who will explain the different sections of the bill. In that way we will have the opportunity of better understanding the sections of the bill.
When I was speaking on the resolution I told the minister that there was general agreement with regard to the different principles which had been enunciated, and I think that was the general opinion of practically all hon. members who spoke. I know objection will be taken to some sections, which I shall not indicate now. There are some sections being deleted which we feel should not be deleted, and I refer to those having to do with the extensions of time given to veterans of
Pension Act
the second world war for the preparation of their cases to be sent to the commission and of their applications for pension.
Some problems are not being considered, and I am sure they should be. It is not my intention this afternoon to discuss them. I know that the Canadian Legion will be before the committee and they will outline some of the problems which we believe should be considered further by this veterans committee, and hon. members will do the same.
The minister has mentioned the fact that the principle in the bill, which was objected to strenuously when the resolution was before the house, is that which dealt with salaries for the chairman, vice-chairman and commissioners being fixed by the governor in council. This matter was discussed nearly three months ago, Mr. Speaker. At that time there was a heated debate in the house, and I had really hoped, and I am sure other hon. members had, that that section would not appear in the bill. The minister tells us that the bill will be sent to the committee with the section included; but, if the committee so desires, it can recommend an amendment.
In my opinion the amendment that he suggests does not go as far as it should. The governor in council should not have the responsibility for fixing salaries. As I said before, this subject will be thoroughly discussed in the committee, but again I should like to point out, as was pointed out by hon. members when the resolution was under discussion, we feel that it does take away from the independence of the commission to have their salaries fixed by order in council. We also feel that it interferes with the supremacy of parliament to have salaries fixed by the governor in council. I know, and all hon. members who have anything to do with veterans affairs or veterans pensions know, that when an application for a pension is made the applicant thinks of the government as being on one side and of himself on the other. He thinks of the government possibly trying to save money by not giving him as large a pension as he thinks he should have. He, being on the other side, feels that he is trying to get justice. In between the governor in council and the individual is the commission, which in his mind, and I am sure in the minds of all, should be absolutely independent. This is the great objection that we take to this particular clause.
The pensioner feels that there should not be even the appearance of any obligation of this commission to the governor in council. This matter will be urged and argued and I hope the minister does not think that the

Pension Act
amendment which he suggested this afternoon will be the only one which this committee can consider. I am satisfied that some members of the committee at least will desire to make such an amendment as will delete entirely this section from the bill, as I feel it should be.

Mr. Chairman, the report just presented by the Minister of Transport has been very interesting, very hopeful. When the bill has been given second reading I presume it will be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines so that we may have the opportunity of examining the railway officials and of finding out all the details in connection with these proposed extensions. In any event,
I place that suggestion before the minister and I hope he will agree to that course being followed. It has been the practice to refer these bills to that committee. In fact, during the present session the bill which was introduced by the Canadian Pacific Railway was referred to and dealt with by that standing committee.
To the official opposition the proposed extensions seem to be in the best interests of the nation. They are based primarily on mineral development in Canada's pre-Cambrian shield which, of course, is one of our great sources of wealth. I was interested today to hear the minister describe the forest assets in the Chibougamau area as well. I had not realized that so much pulp timber was available. I had thought that these extensions depended almost entirely on the mineral wealth of the areas through which they would run.
The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys tell me that in the Chibougamau area there is now one producing mine known as Opemiska Copper Mines Limited. The

minister referred to it in his opening remarks.
I am told that the production through the mill in December of last year was about 400 tons of ore a day, the ore being largely copper with a small gold content. Then there is another property, namely Campbell Chi-bougamau Mines Limited which is not yet in the production stage but which I understand is planning to mill 1,700 tons a day. There again the ore is largely copper with a small gold content. The Department of Mines and Technical Surveys report a further promising property known as Chibougamau Explorers which, however, has not yet developed to the stage where one can forecast the amount of production.
There is one other feature about this Chibougamau development which the minister did not mention, namely the fact that the Eastern Smelting and Refining Company Limited is to build a nickel-copper smelter and refinery at Chicoutimi. I may have misunderstood him, but I did not hear him make any reference whatever to such a plant.

speechtext:
This plant too is extremely important. As a party, Conservatives believe that these resources should be used in Canada to the maximum possible extent in order to provide work for the Canadian people. We hope this ore will be smelted in Canada. Chicoutimi is one of the national harbours of Canada and we should be extremely glad to see it get this additional development.
I was somewhat concerned about the minister's statement that the work on the line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien is to be delayed. Apparently it is not the intention to start building from both ends at once, a procedure which would seem to be the ordinary one in the construction of these branch lines. If I followed the minister correctly, the plan is to build from Beattyville up to Chibougamau this year and then to let the other part of the line, which is 139 miles in length, wait until it can be ascertained whether or not construction should be carried out. If this plan is as good as the minister makes out it is, I can see no reason why the whole railway should not be built right through from Beattyville to St. Felicien, and the whole job finished 83276-292
Canadian National Railways rather than having half of it done and then letting the other half wait until perhaps some time later on when it might be done. That procedure does not seem to be a particularly satisfactory one.
The minister intimated that the Canadian National Railways have investigated this whole development and have received guarantees of traffic from different industries. That is a wise course to follow and it is the course which they followed in connection with the extension from Sherridon to Lynn Lake in northern Manitoba and from Terrace to Kiti-mat on the west coast. It seems to be the plan followed now by the railways whenever they put in an extension. The Canadian Pacific Railway also had a guarantee before they asked for a bill permitting them to build a branch line from Havelock to Nephton in the province of Ontario. But when the minister came to the branch line in Ontario from Hillsport to Manitouwadge lake, he said nothing whatever about any guarantees from the industries in that area. Apparently the railway company has not obtained any guarantee of traffic from those industries. The reason may be that they consider there is going to be so much traffic anyway that it is unnecessary to get a guarantee. However, I would ask the minister to explain to the committee, before this resolution goes through, just why it is that no guarantee has been obtained in that case.
I realize that the Manitouwadge lake area is a promising district as well. I understand that the main property there is owned by a company known as General Engineering Company and that though they are not yet in production they hope to produce 5,000 tons of concentrates a day. There the minerals are copper, zinc and silver. I also understand that the officials of that company gave evidence before a committee of the Ontario legislature this spring to the effect that the number of employees would run between 750 and 1,750 and that in from 5 to 15 years the town is expected to have a population of from 5,000 to 15,000 people. This is therefore no small development. I also understand that by February of this year, which was only a short time after the initial discovery, 3,600 claims had been staked in this area over a length of 70 miles. This looks like an extremely wealthy mineral area.
I hope that the members of the House of Commons and the Canadian people, in their thinking, are now past the stage where they do not want any more railways built. For a good many years that has been the attitude, that because Canada had overbuilt in the earlier part of this century we should put a stop to building further railways. Because of
4602	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways that attitude of mind it has been very difficult to get railways built where they should be built. But now we seem to be getting into a new era where we are willing to have railways built in the areas that need development. I have here the report of the royal commission on transportation, known as the Turgeon commission, which reported three years ago in 1951. They dealt with the Chibougamau lake project. The reference will be found at page 133 and I propose to read what they had to say. It reads as follows:
In the year 1948 the Canadian National Railways completed the construction of a line about forty miles in length from Barraute to Rapide des Cedres in the Abitibi region, Quebec. The representative of the Abitibi economic planning council appeared before the commission to submit that the Canadian National Railways should continue construction to Chibougamau lake, through Bachelor lake, a distance of about 165 miles. The commission has since been informed that the Canadian National Railway Company is considering this matter and is awaiting further information to decide whether potential traffic will warrant the building of the extension.
It has taken six years to get around to the building of this extension. In the meantime apparently the government of Quebec has built a road from lake St. John to the Chibougamau region, and I think should be given great credit for its development work in the northern part of Quebec. The same is true of course of the government of Ontario. They have been very progressive in their approach to the development of the northern part of their province. These two great provinces of Canada have set the rest of the country a very good example in the way in which they have gone about the development of their northern territories.
The commission made a general recommendation respecting the building of new railways in Canada which I think sets out what should be the policy of any Canadian government. It is to be found at page 130 of the report. First of all they refer to the situation in the United States which is a good deal different from that pertaining in Canada because the Americans have not a great area to the north that has not yet been opened up. In Canada by far the largest part of our territory is north of that part of the country where most of the people live. The commission had this to say:
In Canada the situation is somewhat different. There is still room for railway expansion where it is called for by the needs of settlers already established in productive areas or by the necessity of making available new areas possessing mineral and other natural resources attainable only by railway. It seems to be generally assumed that most, if not all, railway expansion in the foreseeable future will be carried on by the government of Canada or by the Canadian National Railways which the government owns.


Incidentally, I do not think I would go as far as to say that the C.N.R. has to build all the new lines. The report continues:
The day of ill-conceived and therefore excessive construction seems to have gone by, and our people can feel reasonably assured that from now on no railway ventures will be undertaken excepting after thorough investigation of each project and always with due regard to the financial commitments involved.
The extensions covered by this resolution seem to qualify under the terms of this recommendation of the commission. I think that some day, Mr. Chairman, we will have to have a railway right across the northern part of Canada. Perhaps that would not be necessary across northern Ontario or northern Quebec, but in western Canada I think, after most of us are gone from the scene, there will be a railway running across the northern part perhaps by way of Lynn Lake and lake Athabasca right across to Stewart on the west coast of British Columbia, or even possibly into the Yukon. I am absolutely certain that the future of this country lies in the north. That is the area in which we are going to make great advances. There will of course be developments in the settled part of Canada, and millions more people will settle in the areas where there are now large settlements. But I believe our real bonanza is to be found in northern Canada, and this party is very much in favour of any reasonable project that will open up the northern part of the nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the people of my own constituency of Villeneuve, as well as those of the constituency of Chapleau, have noted with great interest the federal government's decision to introduce the necessary legislation to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct lines of railway to facilitate the development of that rich mining belt which extends from Senneterre to the districts of Chibougamau and Mistassini. They are also pleased to learn that the construction of the railway will be extended to St. Felicien in the lake St. John district. The people of northwestern Quebec and the lake St. John district are very grateful to the Minister of Transport and the Canadian government for having taken that decision.
The extension of the Canadian National Railway line from Beattyville to Chibougamau and St. Felicien will not only be beneficial to our national system of railways but will also be of great advantage to the province and to the country as a whole. It will contribute to the development of a district which is in itself almost as large as the whole of those parts of western Quebec and

Lake St. John together which are settled at the present time. It will add to the general welfare of our own district and that of Lake St. John. It will permit the utilization of a tremendous amount of natural resources which otherwise would not be transformed into national wealth.
It is the opinion of all economists that the extension of the railway line from Beattyville to Chibougamau is more particularly of the utmost importance. It will be built in a general northeast direction and it will follow the centre of a belt rich not only in minerals but also in timber stands and fertile land.
The fact that the geological structure of that region which extends from Senneterre to Chibougamau and Mistassini is favourable to important mining developments is indicated by the astonishing results already attained. Prospectors and mining companies have long since started to survey the district, even in the absence of any adequate system of transportation. Many good mining prospects have been discovered at Wedding river, Cameron lake, Burge lake, Bachelor lake, Opawica, Opemiska, Chibougamau and Mistassini. Large-scale explorations have been carried out in some of those areas and important deposits have been outlined. Opemiska Copper Mines (Quebec) Limited is already in production. Campbell Chibougamau Mines Limited, Merrill Island Mining Corporation and Chibougamau Explorers Limited will be producing within the next two years.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra mentioned Eastern Metals. He said that there may be a danger that if we do not encourage that new industry, some of these concentrates may have to be treated in the United States. I shall tell the hon. member that he does not have to worry. The idea of building a line from Chibougamau to Beattyville is to permit these mining companies operating in that district to ship their concentrate to the Noranda smelter in Noranda, in the constituency of Villeneuve, in the province of Quebec, Canada.
Many other companies such as O'Brien, Dome Burge, Lake Goldfields, Empire Oil, Siscoe, Obalski and others have discovered and outlined interesting deposits of minerals and are presently waiting for adequate means of transportation in order to start their operations. Moreover, if we look at a map of the district we can easily see that prospecting is only beginning. The geological structure of that region is formed by three belts of volcanic rocks of the Keewatin type which meet at their extremes and are separated by masses of intrusive rocks. Those green rocks of the Keewatin type contain such base metals as copper, nickel, lead and zinc as well as 83276-292^
Canadian National Railways precious metals. The richest ore deposits are found near the contacts of the greenstone with the intrusive rocks, above all in the zone of the least resistance and of major faults. Those faults are frequent in the region and geologists have even observed a major fault which crosses the said territory from the southwest to the northeast along the route of the proposed railway.
Under present conditions, research work is difficult and expensive. The construction of the proposed railroad will make it easier and will greatly reduce its cost. Furthermore, the realization of this project will facilitate access to the territories immediately to the south and to the north of that belt where geological formations are also favourable to mineral deposits. According to conservative estimates, the forests of that section contain at least 30 million cords of merchantable timber ready for exploitation. The composition of that forest, the high quality and the accessibility of that timber contribute to increase its value.
Only the construction of the proposed railroad makes it possible for the economical exploitation of those forest resources. The whole reserve of 30 to 50 million cords will be accessible to the proposed railroad. Moreover, a large portion of that forest has attained maturity. It ought to be exploited within a reasonable length of time because it represents an unproductive capital asset, always exposed to partial destruction. A program of rational exploitation will permit the transportation of one-half of one million to one million cords annually.
There are also extensive tracts of favourable land for farming in that district. Many townships containing thousands of acres can be profitably devoted to agriculture and a great number of settlers can be established in that area. Potential waterpower is estimated at more than one million horsepower, and it is well distributed within the region.
Mr. Chairman, I can visualize the tremendous development which will take place along that railroad line once it is built. I can foresee what will happen because for the last 30 years I have been virtually living in that district, and I know it almost as well as my own constituency of Villeneuve. In the immediate vicinity of the area that the railroad will pass, I have surveyed many hundred miles of lines from one end of the district to the other. I have established meridian lines, parallel of latitude, township lines and I have surveyed and staked more than 1,000 mining claims.
In the not too far distant future along the proposed railroad, there will be thriving

Canadian National Railways centres at Barraute, Barville, Despinassy, Champneuf, Bartouille, Laas, Beattyville, Rapide des Cedres, Quevillon, Wedding Lake, Cameron, Burge Lake, Sullivan River, Bachelor Lake, Opawica, Laparent, Opemiska, Lac Cache and Chibougamau.
Some of those places are already nice little villages but they will be growing fast. Others are only what you call locations on the map. There are no people there yet but they will soon come and they each will be the pioneers in their own capacity-the miners, the settlers, the missionaries and the educators, the civic minded citizens, the professional and the business men. Those will be the ones who will really open and develop another new section of our northern reaches.
Each one of those new settlements will have to be provided with its churches, schools, post office, civic, medical and business centres. There will be opportunities for all and I predict that within the next 15 years the population of that area will be well over 50,000 people. I am not exaggerating when I say this, Mr. Chairman. We have only to look back on what happened in northwestern Quebec during the last 30 years to realize that what took place there can be duplicated in even a shorter period of time.
Thirty years ago, during the summer of 1924, as a student, I had the opportunity of going on a survey expedition in the very part of Quebec that I now have the honour of representing in this parliament. At that time in the whole of the constituency of Villeneuve there were less than 1,000 people. There were no roads, no railroads, no airfields, fewer industrial centres or large communities. The only two places which were inhabited at the time were the actual parish of La Motte and the prospecting centre of Rouyn-Noranda.
Today, in the same district which is now the constituency of Villeneuve, we find a thriving population of more than 70,000 people, some of them cultivating rich farms located along the northern part of the constituency, others working at the gold, silver, copper, lead and zinc mines located in Val d'Or, Malartic, Cadillac, Duparquet and Rouyn-Noranda areas. Where 30 years ago there was nothing but bush, muskeg, rock and water, we now have progressive towns and cities, rich mines and productive farm lands of which we can be proud. And what is more important, we have a group of people who, as pioneers, took up the challenge offered by that part of the shield in Quebec. The fact that they met it successfully has procured substantial benefits for every home in the province. Not only does northern Quebec provide the whole of Canada with
fMr. Dumas.]
metals, lumber, pulpwood, farm products and furs, but the growing population of that district, its purchasing power and its needs, stimulate the manufacturing industries of our cities to the south.
Nor has northern Quebec yielded all its richness to the province and the rest of Canada. The geological structure of those adjoining areas where the proposed railroad will be built, their similarity to other districts to the south whose mineral resources are abundant, the discoveries already made, the quality and accessibility of vast timber limits, the potential water power, as well as the unanimous opinion of the experts regarding the possibilities of that region, entitle us to forecast that this district will become an essential factor in the economy of our province.
The construction of this railroad line is an important step toward the economic conquest of the Canadian shield which contains immense natural resources that are essential to the welfare of Canada and its people.

Mr. Chairman, one of the thrills of being a Canadian is the realization that the story of the development of this country is not confined to the past. I am sure that all of us are fascinated by the realization that we possess tremendous natural resources which are largely untapped, and that they hold for us and for those who will follow us a great future. It has been the privilege of many of us who sit in the House of Commons today to support other measures similar to this one which were brought down in years gone by for the purpose of helping to open up and develop areas in this country which are rich in mineral, timber and other natural resources. We of this group are pleased that this resolution has been brought in and it will have our support.
I think hon. members generally will not be surprised if I take advantage of this opportunity to draw attention once again to the fact that although most of the members of this house, indeed, all but those of this group, subscribe wholeheartedly to the notion that private enterprise can do everything, despite that fact there come occasions such as this when the private enterprisers of this country look to the government, look to public enterprise, for the expenditure of public money to make possible the development of our great natural resources. Some day the lesson that flows from that fact will be learned and put into practice for the benefit of all our people.
Since this resolution has the support of most hon. members it need not be the occasion for a lengthy debate and I shall not repeat the things which have been said by

previous speakers. But there is one request I should like to make of the Minister of Transport. As the minister knows, there have been various complaints in recent years when other lines of railway were being constructed concerning labour conditions. I need not go into detail and I admit that when some of the charges that have been made were investigated they were found, in the opinion of the investigators at any rate, to be exaggerated.
Nevertheless there were complaints in connection with the labour conditions in connection with the construction of the line that was built from Sherridon to Lynn Lake. Those complaints involved certain companies to whom contracts had been let and in some instances they also involved activities of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
While something else I want to say is not directly related to this bill I think it is close enough that I should be permitted to refer to it in passing. From time to time complaints have reached some of us concerning labour conditions in connection with this same Welch company to which I have been referring in connection with contracts let to them by the Canadian National Railways. In the main, these complaints are of two types. The union affected does not like the way in which its collective agreements are by-passed when track or maintenance work is let out to a company of that kind. The other complaint is that labour conditions under this company are not very satisfactory. As a matter of fact I have on my desk at the present time a letter dealing with some of these unsatisfactory labour conditions.
I mention this fact so that I may ask the Minister of Transport to take up this matter with the Canadian National Railways when the time comes to build these lines of railway. I ask the minister to see to it that the Canadian National Railways does not leave itself open to criticism with respect to labour conditions and with respect to the conditions under which workmen will have to live and work in connection with the building of these railways.
These are important lines of railway. It is good that they are being built. Let us see to it that in the building of them those who do the hard work in this northern country have the best possible labour conditions. Let us see that none of the principles which we have accepted as right and proper in this field, including those principles which are covered in our various labour codes, are violated or by-passed in any way.
With these few remarks, I may say that we are glad to support this resolution.

I have also some knowledge of the Manitou-wadge discovery and development which has been one of the sensations of the mineral world and in which many of my constituents who are engaged in engineering have had a part. This district holds great possibilities. I am advised that the tonnage indicated by diamond drilling is in the neighbourhood of ten million tons and that it would not be unreasonable to expect that there would be a tonnage from one of the original discovery properties of between two and four thousand tons a day. I suppose that that will produce a relatively large volume of freight in the form of concentrates which will have to go to the smelter unless one becomes possible in the camp itself. There are other properties which show great promise and there are many prospects under development.
This kind of railway operation is one which appeals to me more particularly when it has to do with the development of mines and forest. I have had some personal experience with the Ontario Northland Railway, formerly the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. This line opened up an area which then had no great economic prospects at the time but it provided a means of access to mines and forest as well as agricultural lands in the northern part of the province. As the minister well knows, it has turned out most successfully, and is now a profitable railway. We have hopes that both of these ventures will turn out in the same way.
There is just one question I should like to raise that occurs to me as I consider the position of the Manitouwadge area. As the minister knows, it lies between the Canadian National railway on the north and the Canadian Pacific railway on the south. It is probably midway between the two. In fact, it will promote the development of mineral deposits in the Chibougamau area and neighbouring districts. That will constitute a further step towards economic conquest of our immense natural resources which are vital to the welfare of our people. The rich mining discoveries in the Chibougamau district are more than enough to warrant this $35 million outlay and no doubt the future will confirm the foresight of our present leaders in introducing this bill which will make it possible to develop and use our natural resources. The Canadian government thus contributes to maintain a high level of national income and that decision will result in a more buoyant and stable Canadian economy.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has just told us that the Canadian National Railways will begin with the Beattyville-Chibougamau stretch of line. The people of the Lake St. John district are most anxious for this work to be started. I am asking the government on this occasion to authorize the Canadian National Railways to begin the two sections at the same time.

The fact that the district is extremely rich in hydroelectric power, should also promote establishment of new ore and metal smelting plants.

Mr. Chairman, I listened carefully, a moment ago, with particular interest and much pleasure, to the appropriate words of explanation which the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) was kind enough to give us in connection with the bill now before the house.
Representations have certainly been made, over the years, to the government in order to obtain construction of this railway. I am glad to be able to say a few words about this bill, so that I may commend the hon. Minister of Transport and the government for their present decision.
The districts of Chibougamau and Lake St. John are, as everybody knows, rich in mineral deposits. It is therefore time, I believe, to give particular credit to the pioneers, to those men who, from the beginning, opened up to civilization this new area full of an abundant wealth that will be profitable, not only to Quebec, but to Canada as a whole.

We must remember that the first to go to the Chibougamau district did so at the cost of great sacrifices, since there were then but two means of transportation, either by water or through the woods with dog teams. They surely deserve much credit and we must pay tribute to their courage as they are primarily responsible for the expansion of this rich mining district in the province of Quebec.
It must also be said, I believe, that private enterprise has contributed up to now its fair share of expenses and sacrifices during the last few years. It seems to me that we must also give credit to the government of the province of Quebec for having understood the need of a carriage road into this remote district and for having spent millions of dollars for the construction of that road. Therefore, it was high time, Mr. Chairman, for the government of Canada to do its share by helping the Canadian National Railways to construct a railway line, so that the ore produced in the Chibougamau district may be shipped more favourably.
The government has yielded to the wishes of the whole province of Quebec but more particularly to the request made last year, on March 2, 1953, if I remember correctly, by a delegation representing the council of economic planning of the Lake St. John district, which submitted at that time, to the government and to the hon. Minister of Transport, a brief carefully prepared by outstanding economists, on the economic advantages to be expected from the construction of that railway line.
I extend my most sincere congratulations to the minister for having introduced the present bill. It does not matter, Mr. Chairman, whether this railway operates, during a certain time, at a loss. Besides, it would not be the first time, for we know that railways have operated at a loss in the past. However, the Canadian National is controlled by the government and the loss brought about by insufficient revenues will be, no doubt, largely compensated by other revenue resulting from the economic expansion that will surely follow its construction.
I am particularly pleased with this bill because it will make transportation easier between the Saguenay-Lake St. John district and my own district, that is, the city of Quebec.
It will first of all contribute to provide work for hundreds of unemployed who ask nothing better than a chance to earn their living honestly and provide for the needs of
Canadian National Railways their family and their children. Secondly, the building of that railroad will increase our national wealth and, thirdly, it will ensure the economic stability of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district.
Mr. Chairman, before concluding my remarks on the matter, may I be permitted to remind the minister-and I hope that in doing so I shall not be out of order-that there is between Quebec and the Lake St. John district another railroad of which mention has been made on several previous occasions in the house. That railroad is in such poor repair that it should be completely rebuilt. The fact that it is possible, on the one hand, to travel from Ottawa to the provincial capital of Quebec, a distance of 289 miles, in six hours while, on the other hand, it takes exactly 10 hours and 35 minutes to go from Quebec to Dolbeau in the Lake St. John district, a distance of only 233 miles, gives a good idea of the pitiable condition of that railroad.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my first word should be one of thanks to the committee for the manner in which it has received this resolution having to do with the construction of two branch lines of the Canadian National Railways, one in the province of Quebec and the other in the province of Ontario. I can only express the hope that the rest of the legislation which I have to bring before parliament this session, and it comprises some seven or eight bills, will receive the same enthusiastic reception.
I do not intend to make any lengthy remarks because I do not think the resolution stage is the place where this should be done, but I think the committee, in view of the temper it is now in, would wish me at least to reply to some of the suggestions made during the course of this debate.
It has been suggested that the bill, when it reaches the appropriate stage, should be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. While it is not the practice to make that kind of announcement at this stage, I think, in view of the manner in which the house has received this resolution, that I should say now that it is the intention to follow the usual practice. As a matter of fact, I believe it would be a serious mistake not to do that because this is a matter which involves many millions of dollars and should be carefully considered by the committee.
At this committee there will be officers of the Canadian National Railways who will be able to discuss with the committee the profitability or non-profitability of the various aspects of the two lines. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra indicated that there

was probably no reason for building the west section alone without at the same time building the eastern section. I think his words were to the effect that he did not think it was satisfactory to build at the west end first and delay the building of the eastern section, that is, St. Felicien to Chibougamau until after. But if the hon. member reads carefully what I said in my opening remarks I do not think he will glean that suggestion from the statements which I made to the house.
The government and the Canadian National Railways consider this whole line as a single enterprise. They believe it will be in the general interests of Canada to build it all. The Canadian National Railways have guarantees and will be able to establish the profitability, the financial betterment to the Canadian National Railways of that part of the line which extends from Beattyville to Chibougamau. As a matter of fact, that is only a continuation of the line they were authorized by parliament to build in 1949, and it has been proven to be profitable. It may be possible, though I do not affirm this, that by the time they complete the construction from Beattyville to Chibougamau, they can begin and continue construction on to St. Felicien, but that will depend upon industrial development in the area at that time. Indeed, it may depend on the industrial development in the immediate future.
My hon. friend referred to the zinc refinery about to be built at Chicoutimi. I hope it will be built, but I have no assurance on that score. The Canadian National Railways have tried on several occasions to have a zinc refinery built at Chicoutimi.

speechtext: Is that zinc or nickel?

speechtext:
Zinc. If that zinc development were forthcoming-if there was private initiative that would establish it-and if there were a guarantee similar to that which I have mentioned in connection with the western part of the line, then there could be no difficulty or no objection about the continuation of the line. It might well be that that position will obtain by the time the line has reached Chibougamau.
Then my hon. friend put a question in connection with the fact that there was no guarantee on the Ontario line from Hillsport to lake Manitouwadge such as there was on the western part of the Quebec line. The reason for that situation is obvious. The position of the Ontario line is so profitable in the eyes of the Canadian National Railways that no guarantee is necessary. I think the hon. member for St. Paul's covered that point perhaps as well as I could do it. The reason is this. In view of the potential traffic which exists in that area, the Canadian

National Railways estimate that the revenues on the Canadian National Railways will be bettered to the extent of $6 million a year by the construction of this line from Hillsport to lake Manitouwadge. In fact, the inbound traffic alone would warrant the construction of the line, let alone the outbound traffic; and the outbound traffic will be far more important than the inbound traffic. As a matter of fact, the minimum amount of traffic required for a profitable position on the Ontario line would be 700 tons per day; and that amount will be more than reached by the potential mining development in that area.
Then another reason why no guarantee is necessary is that this is in a completely different section of the Pre-Cambrian shield than are the Quebec lines. The Quebec lines are in entirely undeveloped country whereas the Ontario line is built almost between two main railway lines, that of the Canadian National Railways and that of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In fact the distance from lake Manitouwadge to the Canadian National Railways is 27 miles and to the Canadian Pacific Railway the distance is a little bit greater. Although I am not too sure just what it is, I think it is perhaps 35 or 40 miles.
To deal with the question raised by the hon. member for St. Paul's, namely whether or not the Canadian Pacific Railway had indicated any interest in the line, I can only say that I am sure they are interested. In fact, any railway company would be interested in that amount of potential traffic. However, they have certainly given no indication to me or, so far as I am aware, to any others connected with the government of their intention to build such a line. I presume, however, that if the Canadian National Railways felt that such a line should be built, they might feel similarly. However, that consideration in itself is not a reason why they should. Even if the Canadian Pacific Railway wanted to construct a branch line into that area, it would be for parliament to decide whether, having regard to the charter which we will, I hope, approve here, they should give a second charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
My friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised the question of labour relations and labour conditions in connection with the subcontracts or the contracts which the Canadian National Railways give on these lines. He referred more particularly to one which had been given in connection with a branch line authorized in the House of Commons from Sherridon to Lynn Lake some two years ago. I remember the charges which were made, I think, by a Winnipeg paper. I brought them to the attention of the Canadian National Railways and they
Canadian National Railways were immediately investigated. I must say that they were highly exaggerated. I do not think there was any doubt about the exaggeration of the conditions under which men were alleged to be working. I also know that the Department of Labour carried out an investigation. The results of both the investigation by the Department of Labour and that by the Canadian National Railways were made public at the same time. However, I am glad the hon. member brought to the attention of the committee the conditions that appertained there. I shall see that the Canadian National Railways officials are made aware of the position-not that they are not already aware of it-and that in granting any contracts or subcontracts, they shall keep in mind the consideration that the general labour conditions should be in accordance with the laws and the labour code of this country.

Emergency Powers Act. I thank my hon. friend for the correction. Under the Emergency Powers Act the governor in council passed an order providing for regulations for the movement of goods in bulk. This order in council has to do with movement by rail and on ships. The legislation referred to in the resolution will be contained in a short bill to be introduced later and seeks to continue for a period of two years only practically the same powers that are contained in that order in council.
As the committee knows, following the appointment of the transport controller there was provision whereby goods in bulk as defined in the regulations could be moved in adequate volume and at the times required. I believe that the transport controller and his assistants have done a very good job. As the situation is now, the transport controller has a representative in Vancouver with one stenographer. There is also a deputy controller in Montreal, and a secretary in Ottawa, because of necessity the transport controller must spend most of his time away from his office here. All told there are but six employees in this branch of the department.
The aim of the transport controller has been to ensure the movement of bulk commodities such as grain and grain products, ore, coal, pulpwood, pulp and timber of all kinds in order to meet export requirements. Since transport control was established there has never been a shortage of box cars in


western Canada to move Canada's grain crop. There have always been approximately fifty thousand cars in the west which is sufficient to keep terminal unloading and cleaning capacity operating efficiently and to meet all export and domestic commitments.
Vessel transportation has been ample to meet all shipping requirements. The transport controller has had tremendous cooperation not only from all rail companies but also from shipping companies. For instance, in 1952-53 exports of the five major Canadian grains together with the grain equivalents of wheat flour, rolled oats and oatmeal, totalled 583,200,000 bushels. This was a new all-time record for foreign shipments of Canadian grain during one crop year, exceeding by 15 per cent the previous high volume established in 1951-52 when over-all exports amounted to 506 million bushels.
In 1952-53, for the second time in their shipping history, the Pacific coast elevators topped 100 million bushels of wheat destined overseas. More than 104 million bushels were exported through these ports to break the record of 103 million bushels set in 1951-52. The same can be said of Canada's Atlantic ports. They also had a record year for wheat, loading out nearly 189 million bushels, 24 per cent more than the previous record of 151 million bushels. The same can be said of the port of Churchill where 8,600,000 bushels of wheat were shipped in the 1952 season and over 10,500,000 bushels in the 1953 season.
As I indicated earlier, all of the transportation agencies, railways, exporters, elevator operators, owners of ocean-going vessels, the federations of agriculture and others, have co-operated with the transport controller to the fullest extent, and I think the committee will be of opinion that it is in the general interests of the trade and commerce of this country that the transport controller be continued in existence so that the movement of these goods in bulk can be carried on efficiently. For that reason I am confident that the resolution will commend itself to the committee.

I believe that these powers were first brought into effect when there really was a shortage of railway box cars compared with the demand for shipment of scrap iron of all kinds, lumber, ferrous metals and grain. The situation today is entirely different. There is an oversupply of box cars and no shortage whatsoever. It may be that these regulations, as they are now constituted, and as I presume they will be in the legislation, are necessary in order to have a fair allocation of box cars to maintain the quota system.
We should not fool ourselves into thinking that the transport controller is really controlling the allocation of box cars. I have heard him say that it is the Canadian wheat board that decides the amount of each kind of grain that it wants. It is the Canadian wheat board that decides the number of box cars of grain it will take from each elevator company. The wheat board informs the railway companies of the amount of grain that is required and the transport controller tells the railway companies to make sufficient box cars available to move that grain.
The trouble is that these powers have not been used in a way that is fair and equitable to the producers in western Canada, and which would allow them to deliver to the elevator of their own choice. As a matter of fact the kind of powers that are embodied in this legislation, whether they are used by the transport controllers or whether they are turned over to the railway companies or some other body, have resulted in definite discrimination in the allocation of box cars and have removed the freedom of choice of elevator company from the producer. Certainly, if the powers in this legislation are to be used in a fair and equitable manner, some very definite changes in policy will have to be made.
I have before me a table of the relative position in the handling of grain in Saskatchewan. These figures are taken from various government publications, and are compiled by the Sanford Evans statistical service of Winnipeg as of March, 1952. These statistics show that when the farmers in Saskatchewan have the opportunity to deliver grain to the elevator of their own choice, their own elevator system, controlling 40-7 per cent of the capacity, obtained 50-4 per cent of the patronage. As the elevators became plugged and as space available in the elevators was made possible only through the allocation of box cars, this allocation resulted in a definite loss of business to that farmer owned organization. There was a gradual and continuing loss until now that elevator system, which has increased its capacity in the intervening years from 40 per cent to 44 per cent, has found its handlings drop from 50 per cent to 45 per cent and according to the current information those handlings are down now to about 43 per cent.

For some considerable time there have been four different statutes which dealt with the rights of different groups of public servants who happened to make inventions which were patentable and for which patents were secured. There were certain provisions in the Patent Act which applied to what I suppose would be described as the ordinary kind of civil servants. Then there were provisions in the National Defence Act which applied to that department and to some extent to the forces. There were also certain provisions in the Atomic Energy Control Act and in the Research Council Act. It was felt by the government that there was a reasonable ground for certain public servants to feel that they were being discriminated against in certain circumstances as opposed to others, and in any event that we ought to have, as soon as it could be conveniently done, uniform legislation applying to all public servants.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill proposes to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act and I will make a further explanation of that in a moment. I introduce this bill in the knowledge that a similar bill has been introduced before. But circumstances have changed since that time, and I believe that some of the factors which at that time seemed so highly debatable can now, in the light of recent developments and future prospects, be introduced and justified to a greater extent than ever before.
The intent and purpose of this measure is outlined clearly in the explanatory notes. The only change sought by the introduction of this measure is the insertion of the words "or Churchill" in the appropriate places in two sections of the act. As the explanatory note states:
The effect of this change will be to permit producers in the area accessible to the port of Churchill to get the advantage of the cheaper freight rates to Churchill, wherever such cheaper rates apply. The implementation of this provision will not involve any increase in expenditure either by the government or by the Canadian wheat board.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to a statement made by Mr. Robbins of the Canadian wheat board speaking at the Hudson Bay Route Association meeting in Moose Jaw on March 4. He said he felt that the farmers in the area accessible to Churchill should have the benefit of the cheaper freight rate to that port as against the port at Fort William. Subsequently a resolution was passed at that meeting which reads as follows:
Be it resolved that the wheat board be requested to credit the individual growers of wheat with the saving in freight that can be made through shipments to Churchill and thus place Saskatchewan
Canadian Wheat Board Act farmers in a similar position to Alberta farmers residing in the preferential freight area of Pacific coast points.
I am tempted at this point to go into all the aspects of the Hudson bay route as it affects and will affect in future the over-all economy of western Canada, but I do not propose to do so. I will rather confine my remarks to the bill before the house at the present time.
Wheat producers in the area accessible to Churchill feel very strongly about the fact that the wheat board has not seen fit to make the port of Churchill a basing point. In other words, we feel that the port of Churchill should be designated a port of delivery for wheat bought by the wheat board, thereby placing us in exactly the same position as those producers in the area accessible to the port of Vancouver and, by the same token, the port at the lakehead. Producers in western Saskatchewan and in Alberta are in a preferential area. That means that if you live on or west of a line roughly through Battleford, instead of shipping your wheat to Fort William you can ship it to Vancouver. You will realize, Mr. Speaker, that as you get farther west your freight rate progressively decreases. If you live east of that line through Battleford and on into Manitoba your freight rate also becomes progressively less as you come closer to the lakehead.
We in the area adjacent to the port of Churchill believe that we should have the same treatment as those producers who live in these two preferential areas. We believe that we have contributed substantial sums of money toward the building of this Churchill project. I do not intend to go into that, except to say, for the benefit of those hon. members who are not too well acquainted with that project, that the government of Canada set aside in western Canada certain lands amounting to approximately 14 million acres. I believe that land was subsequently sold for some $42 million and that money was spent on this so-called Churchill project. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) indicated some time ago that up to 1945 the dominion government had spent some $51 million on this Churchill project, and that of course included $6 million spent at Port Nelson, which was subsequently abandoned in favour of the port at Churchill. We believe that out of that sum of $51 million we contributed something like $42 million toward that project. In the light of that we think we have a claim to any benefits which may accrue from the cheaper freight rates to the port of Churchill.
I am well aware that the minister will probably criticize that statement and point out, quite rightly, that any savings made

Canadian Wheat Board Act because of cheaper freight rates go into wheat board revenues and that such savings will eventually be reflected in the final payments made by the wheat board. That statement is quite correct, but the same is true of the grain hauled to the port of Vancouver and Fort William. Any savings made there go into the general revenue of the wheat board and are distributed fairly to all the members.
However, in addition to that, those people in these preferential areas gain something over and above that because of the fact that they pay a lower freight rate than we do. To emphasize the problem further, I would point out that the producers in the Melfort and Wadena areas of Saskatchewan, for example, had a great deal of their grain shipped to Churchill, yet they paid the freight based on the Fort William rate. I will admit that the freight paid on wheat sent to Churchill at the present time does not constitute a very great burden. As a matter of fact, I believe that in the most preferred area the cost is four cents per hundred and that is the best price anyone in that accessible area could expect to get. Of course, as you go farther away from the preferred area it falls from four cents to three, and so on. In other words, as you get near the fringe area the differential is not so very much. The Saskatchewan wheat pool in March of last year made an estimate of the benefits which would accrue from the cheaper freight rate if that area and the port of Churchill had been designated a basic point for the wheat board.
Here is the way it would have worked out. All companies combined shipped some 11 million bushels of wheat last year. Of that total, 5,748 bushels came from outside the designated area; 438,453 bushels came from the so-called fringe area around the outside where there was only one cent of differential in freight rate; 1,975,216 bushels came from an area with a preference of two cents; 2 million and some hundred thousand bushels came from an area where the differential was three cents; and 360,040 bushels came from the most preferred area where they would have got a preference of four cents per hundred pounds. I know that the western farmers simply do not understand it and I wish it could be explained more clearly for their benefit.
There are one or two other points. I remember that in opposing such a bill on other occasions the minister used certain arguments that in my opinion are not as valid today as they were then because of changed conditions. One argument that the minister used in October, 1949, was that wheat had to be kept at strategic points so that it would be available immediately for current needs and demands. That was certainly a good argument on that occasion. We were operating under the world wheat contracts then and wheat had to be placed at strategic points. I might say that this fortunate condition does not exist any more. In those days wheat could be delivered freely. There was a market for wheat and a shortage of wheat then compared with now. Wheat is not now moving with the same speed and we do not have to worry about strategic points.
Another argument that the minister used was that we could not afford to keep wheat stored at Churchill because it was an expensive business. That also was true in those times, but as my hon. friend has pointed out we now have to store wheat willy-nilly somewhere, and not only are we not avoiding the storage of wheat at Churchill but we are in the position where we wish we had more room at Churchill for wheat to be stored under almost any conditions.
I also remember that the minister said that at that time only 12J per cent of the actual wheat grown in this area, which would be the area around Churchill if it were made a basing point, was actually shipped through the port of Churchill. That condition has now been changed because with the increase in the amount shipped to approximately 11 million bushels I would venture to say that the percentage of wheat in that particular area shipped through Churchill must have doubled. The figure is now 11 million bushels compared with 5 million bushels in those days. Therefore if this measure had any validity at all at that time it has more validity now.
There is also the fact that we are going to have more wheat at Churchill and that we are, I am afraid, going to have a greater

carryover and more wheat stored in this country for a period of a year or two at least. If the plans for storage go ahead we will have storage there of 5 million bushels instead of the present 2,500,000 bushels. Therefore there will be more wheat available and ready. As my friend has pointed out, the elevators there are full now even in winter. But under ordinary circumstances we would at least expect to have wheat delivered there starting in May or June, and certainly in time so that the elevators would be filled ahead of the coming of the ships in September.
The relative price of the handling at Churchill as compared with Port Arthur and Fort William I feel has some bearing on this matter. The minister himself admitted that, and I am quoting now from page 595 of Hansard for October 6, 1949. The former member for Melfort said:
... if a favourable price is obtained for wheat at the port of Churchill under the world contract,-
We were under a world contract at that time.
-a price in excess of the price at Port Arthur or Fort William, then I think it is doubly necessary that the people adjacent to that port should get some advantage from that price.
The minister replied:
X would agree.
For those reasons then, Mr. Chairman, I am supporting the bill advanced by my colleague.

speechtext:
In adding a few words in support of this Bill No. 441, I think it is clear to the house now that the intention of the bill is only to grant this privilege on freight rates to the areas within reach of Churchill, in the same manner as rates now apply to Fort William, Port Arthur and Vancouver. The effect of that would be to permit producers in the area accessible to the port of Churchill to get the advantage of cheaper freight rates wherever such cheaper rates would apply. The implementation of the provision would not involve any increased expenditure by the government or the Canadian wheat board and therefore we see little reason for not implementing it.
At this time I believe attention should be given to the facilities at the port of Churchill, because of its great importance as a port, its value to Canada as a nation and the development of the northern part of Canada, both economically and for defence as the whole economic and military picture of the world develops. The constituency that I represent would be in that area designated, perhaps only the small outer fringe of that area, but at the same time we feel that in justice to that area Churchill should be given
Canadian Wheat Board Act that advantage. It seems only right that the port of Churchill and the people shipping there should have the same opportunities and privileges as are available to the people shipping to other points.
The matter of grain in the world today, particularly in western Canada, is a subject that is attracting particular attention of the people involved in this business because of the fact that expanding production seems to be a sort of constant thing now. With the changing techniques in the production of wheat, with the use of chemical weed killers and with better facilities, we are able to grow more and better wheat than we have ever grown before. Unfortunately this is true not only in Canada; other countries are learning how to grow wheat more effectively and more efficiently. The result has been that markets for Canada's wheat are gradually declining. It is, therefore, necessary that we look to every facility we can for the storing of our grain.
It appears that within 90 days we are going to be faced, we hope, with another big crop in the west. The problem of storage is then going to tax us, and it will be difficult. I believe I have advocated before in this house that preparations should be made now to have storage facilities available so that this grain can be obtained at the place and time we need it. Statements have been made that some of us seem to look upon a large crop as a calamity. I do not believe any of us have ever said that. The only thing that has been calamitous, so far as the farmer is concerned, has been his inability to deliver grain. If the establishment of storage space at Churchill and other places in Canada will help alleviate that situation, it will be of benefit to the farmer and others as well.
I believe that most of the arguments concerning the value of this bill have been presented. There is nothing more that can usefully be added. I will just say that for the good of Canada and as a means of aiding in making preparations for a situation that is rapidly developed, this would be a good move. It would give some equity to those people who ship grain to that area, and we would like to give it our full support.

have listened with a great deal of interest to the presentation of my neighbours from Saskatchewan in connection with this bill. While my constituency is not in an area that would be directly affected by the change in the bill, I must indicate at this time that I am vitally interested in anything that would affect the extent of the commercial activity at Churchill. The port of Churchill is in the province of Manitoba, and Manitobans

Canadian Wheat Board Act whether they live in the south of the province or in the north, are vitally concerned with any move that would promote increased use of the port facilities.
The progress of the port of Churchill has been comparatively slow. That has been due to several factors. There is the basic problem, of course, of the battle against the elements because the port is located so far to the north. As has been indicated in the discussion this afternoon, the period of activity each year is relatively short. Notwithstanding that fact, there has been gradual expansion in the length of the season, particularly since the end of the war and the availability of modern electronic navigational aids. As the situation improves in this regard, no doubt maximum benefits will be derived from the use of the port facilities at Churchill.
There has been also the battle against vested interests in this country. It has been a long, uphill struggle to get recognition of the port as a suitable site for commercial activities in Canada. Gradually the resistance is being broken down. This afternoon some reference was made to the problem of diversion charges. This is the question in which I have been interested since I came to this house, and like other members from the wheat growing areas I find it difficult to understand why this diversion charge on grain flowing through the port of Churchill has been perpetuated from year to year. It seems to me that an unnecessary financial burden is being placed upon the use of the port. It seems to me that it is one small surviving unnecessary discouragement to the expanding use of the port facilities.
As I listened to the discussion I came to the conclusion that the bill as put forward by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) this afternoon is one step forward in the development of Churchill as a channel of commerce to and from this continent and hence I rise to speak in support of it. There is every possibility that one of the difficulties of a wider use of the Churchill facilities for two-way traffic will be overcome. There is no doubt at all that in the not too far distant future the port will be used to export the rich ore resources that are being discovered and exploited in the northern part of our province.
With the doubling of the storage capacity of Churchill this year there will be an even greater possibility than heretofore of more incoming traffic from European countries. It


seems to me that the proposal in this bill to equalize freight rates and to place Churchill in line with the other major ports of this country is just another step forward in the progress that has been made down through the years toward a more adequate use of the excellent port facilities at Churchill. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, bills in similar terms to this bill have been debated in this house on other occasions, particularly in 1949 and 1950. I suggest that the real situation has not changed greatly since those debates took place. The proposal is that an area be designated as tributary to the port of Churchill and for which Churchill would be the basing point for freight rates. It has been said that this departure would cause no expense to the government and no expense to the wheat board, but I would point out that it would cause expense to farmers who were not within that particular designated area. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) says that his people are not concerned, but I suggest that if this bill goes through they would be concerned because they would pay their portion of the expense involved in making Churchill a basing point.
It is proposed that about forty to fifty million bushels of wheat would be based on Churchill, that is, there would be that much wheat grown in the logical area tributary to Churchill on the basis of existing freight rates. Although the port has been handling more business each year and is creating new records-last year was quite a step ahead- unfortunately it has never been able to handle as much as eleven million bushels during a shipping season. Obviously there would be in addition some thirty to forty million bushels of wheat enjoying the freight rate to Churchill even though the wheat board would be paying the extra charge involved in shipping that grain to where it would actually go, namely Fort William-Port Arthur.
On the ten and a half to eleven million bushels that actually moved to Churchill last year there would have been a saving to the farmers within the designated area, but there was in fact no real saving to the wheat board. While there would have been a theoretical saving of $169,000 in freight rates, there was a payment made on the grain that moved to Churchill of an amount within $1,000 of the first amount in the form of diversion charges. So that we are asked to create a situation by legislation that does not really exist.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister has often
created situations that did not exist.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We did create another basing point at Vancouver. This is a fairly recent development; I think it is within the time I have been in the house. However, we have a factual situation at Vancouver. The points within the designated area with freight rates favourable to Vancouver actually ship their grain to Vancouver. It is only correct that farmers in that area should have any benefits that accrue from pricing on the basis of Vancouver rates. All their grain actually goes there.
There is an area along the dividing line between rates tributary to Vancouver and rates tributary to Port Arthur where circumstances often make it desirable to ship grain to the port which is not the cheaper as far as freight rates are concerned. For example, because of the record movement of wheat from Vancouver at the present time and the limited movement from Port Arthur we have shifted the boundary east by several hundred miles. Today points as far east as Regina are shipping to the Pacific coast even though the freight rate to the lakehead is three or four cents cheaper. We are doing that so that the quota system may be worked out fairly. The wheat board is paying the extra cost. In other words, the man in Regina is being paid on the basis of a freight rate to Fort William when his grain is actually being shipped to Vancouver.
I have outlined a situation which we believe works out to the benefit of all concerned. It is a temporary situation and we think it is justified under present circumstances. But I do not think it could be justified to establish an artificial situation so that the man within a designated area will continue to be paid more for his wheat when we know that the greater portion of the amount that is paid would come out of the pool as a whole, rather than represent a direct saving on the shipment of that grain to Churchill.
So you have two situations. One situation is where you have fifty million bushels in a designated area where the rates would be favourable to Churchill but to where you could ship only ten million bushels; that being the present handling capacity of that port. The other situation involved is that on the ten million bushels shipped, the saving in freight is actually offset in full by diversion charges that must be paid if any grain is to be shipped to Churchill. You ask: Why do we not have diversion charges on grain shipped to Vancouver? The reason is that elevator systems are organized to ship to
Canadian Wheat Board Act Vancouver. For example, the Alberta wheat pool terminal elevator at Vancouver is supported by a line of country elevators owned by the same company in Alberta. The United Grain Growers terminal elevator at Vancouver is also supported by a line of country elevators in Alberta owned by that company. There are other elevators owned by other elevator interests which are in the same position. For example, the Richardson firm built a terminal elevator in Vancouver and own country elevators in Alberta to support that elevator.
I am sorry there is so much difficulty about understanding the reason for diversion charges. The government owns grain elevators. We own a grain elevator at Fort William. We do not operate that elevator. Why do we not operate the elevator? Because it is not supported by a line of country elevators, and so that it may be operated, we lease it to the McCabe Grain Company who have a line of country elevators and are able to support the terminal elevator.
We have an elevator in Prince Rupert that was closed up for a number of years. Why? Because the government had no line of country elevators to gather grain for that terminal and to support it with shipments from the country. It takes a very considerable investment to establish a balanced system of country and terminal elevators. It is no good building a terminal unless you have country elevators; and if you have country elevators you do not get the full earning power out of them unless you can ship to your own terminal. Systems have been built up on that basis; investments are made in that way. They are not made by greedy capitalists; they are often made by the farmers themselves. I suppose the pool chains of grain elevators are far and away the biggest chains. The pools have a great investment in those chains, and if you say to the Alberta wheat pool: "You cannot ship this grain to your own terminal. It is true, you built a terminal at Vancouver so that you could get the earnings from your country elevators. We are not going to allow that; we are going to say that you must ship from country elevators that you own in Alberta to the government elevator at Prince Rupert." Well, the pool would say: "Is that fair? This system is built up to operate as a unit. We are entitled to handle grain at Vancouver that we collect in our country elevators in Alberta". I say, "Well, it is not fair, no, and you are entitled to a diversion charge equivalent to about the earnings that you would have made on the grain had it been shipped to Vancouver". It is exactly the same situation if grain is being diverted to a flour mill.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
Grain is collected by an elevator company, and that company would normally expect to deliver the grain to its own terminal. If it is denied the privilege of shipping to its own terminal, it is the usual custom to pay a diversion charge on the grain. That is a reasonable expense. The principle has been agreed to over the years for a great many years. It is a logical expense in connection with shipments from privately-owned country elevators in Manitoba or Saskatchewan to Churchill.
I think therefore that this bill should be defeated. It creates an illogical situation. It gives a few people benefits to which the facts of life do not entitle them. However, I think my hon. friend, if he would like a suggestion for a bill in the future, is overlooking the real advantages of shipping to Churchill. There are earnings at Churchill, not in delivering grain to Churchill, but in shipping grain from Churchill. There is a benefit of about 9 cents a bushel on ocean freight rates from Churchill to European markets, as against shipments from Fort William to European markets. And he might logically say that that benefit belongs to the farmers in this designated area. Well, I still think that would be a poor argument. It would be a better argument, but after all we ship grain from where we can and to our best available advantage. Grain is a national problem. We build national ports; we spend taxpayers' money, great sums of it, in building facilities to market the grain crops of Canada. The advantages shift from year to year. Ocean freight rates have a good deal to do with differentials, and the savings are not the same from year to year. Therefore I think the present practice of marketing grain where we can, pooling the sums recovered and distributing them among all the producers, is a fair method of handling the marketing of Canadian wheat.
I just mentioned that suggestion so that my hon. friend will not bring this bill down again. We have had this proposal too many times. I do not think it is a logical bill; but if he really wants to get a debate on this subject he may lay claim to the extra 9 cents a bushel that represents the savings on shipments from Churchill. He might get some supporters. I do not know that I have anything else to offer other than to say I hope this bill will be defeated.
