speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 375, to amend the Research Council Act.
He said: The amendments to the Research Council Act which this bill proposes are fundamentally designed to remove certain ambiguities and clarify certain financial arrangements that have assumed greater importance as the research council has grown in size. These amendments do not change in any fundamental way the principles and procedures which have guided the council in its operations over the years, and which, I think, have made possible the very effective work which that institution has been able to do in the promotion, organization and coordination of scientific and industrial research in Canada.
As there appears to be considerable interest at the moment in the broad aspects of industrial research in this country, I think it would be appropriate for me to say something at this time about how research is organized from the government standpoint, what is being achieved and what we may look forward to. I realize, as will all hon. members, that the research council is by no means responsible for all the scientific and industrial research but it does have very broad responsibilities and has had a great influence in guiding, directing and coordinating such activities over the past two decades. There can be no doubt about the value of scientific research to the country's industrial strength, as well as to its health, prosperity and well-being.
World war II demonstrated our nation's dependence on research and I have never heard in a debate in this house or elsewhere any question of the value of that research. The only difference of opinion is on the scale of support, and the best methods of coordinating the various activities. The important point to realize is that large-scale industrial research as we know it today is

a very recent phenomenon in the Englishspeaking countries. It is true that by the turn of the century Germany had built a large industrial empire on fundamental and applied research facilities, but before world war I there were relatively few large research laboratories either in government or in private industry on this continent. Between the world wars, however, major industrial companies in the United States such as the General Electric Company, Westinghouse Company, Dupont Chemical Company and the American Telegraph and Telephone Company built up very large competent scientific research laboratories. The same thing was true in England. But in Canada no corresponding development took place. This is quite understandable and was due to the fact that most sizeable industrial companies that expanded in Canada during those years were branch factories, and those in turn were dependent on research facilities in either the United States or Great Britain.
There were a few exceptions such as the Shawinigan Company, and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, but generally speaking just before world war II broke out one could say that there were few real research laboratories in Canadian industrial plants.
Just to fill out the picture I would like to give the following figures which were contained in an address in 1949 by the then president of the national research council. The figures were given to indicate in a general way the expenditures and activities in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada just before the outbreak of war. I realize that such figures are difficult to obtain in precise form but these difficulties, I think, can be taken as representing at least the order of magnitude of activity and prove the point I wish to make.
In 1938-39 government expenditures, which of course reflect activities and facilities on scientific and industrial research in the three countries, were on a per capita basis almost the same: from 40 to 50 cents. On the other hand, the per capita expenditures by industry were markedly different in the three countries: $1.70 in the United States, somewhere between 30 and 50 cents in the United Kingdom; and about 20 cents per capita in Canada.
It will be seen then that in 1938-39 in the United States private industry was supporting industrial research on a scale eight to ten times greater on a per capita basis, and perhaps 100 times greater on the basis of total dollars, as compared with what was being done in Canada. Further, in the United States at that time private industry was spending three to four times as much as the
Research Council Act
government, while in Canada government expenditures on research were over twice that of industry.
During and since the war the relative burdens of research expenditures have changed radically, particularly in the United States where government expenditures are now approximately equal to those of industry. While the picture here has also changed, and is changing, it is necessary, when considering how industrial research has developed in Canada, to keep in mind the comparative lack of private industrial research facilities in this country before world war II.
Let me illustrate by mentioning one problem we faced in 1939, namely the development and production of radar equipment. In developing such equipment in the United Kingdom and United States it was possible to place development contracts with the large research laboratories of private industries. In Canada, as I have said, comparable industry had no research facilities and, owing to war security restrictions, our branch factories were cut off from all contacts with the laboratories of the parent companies in such military work. As a consequence the development work in radar had to be organized by the national research council, and a crown company, Research Enterprises Limited, had to be set up to do the engineering development and production. The same thing had to be done to produce optical glass and many other special devices, and for work in the field of atomic energy.
The situation was slightly different in some of the chemical industries, especially those involved in the manufacture of explosives; but generally speaking when special and novel research and development were required the primary facilities could be found only in our government laboratories. As the result of our war activities the situation has changed a great deal, and many private industries are now doing good research and development work. But even yet it has been my experience that when one desires to place large development contracts with industry it is usually not possible to find facilities comparable to those which exist in the United States and United Kingdom.
During world war II research expenditures and activities went up phenomenally in all countries. Our expenditures in Canada for government research are at least ten times greater than in 1939, and a comparable expansion was experienced in the United States and United Kingdom. The result is that today our government expenditures and activities on scientific and industrial research are of a very different order of magnitude than those of 1939. For instance, it is I think
4624	HOUSE OF
Research Council Act
interesting to note that in the matter of dollars and cents the Canadian government today is spending more than the total sum spent by the United States in 1938-39, and it will be recalled that the United States at that time had a high reputation in this field. Our current expenditures are likewise several times the total expenditures in Great Britain in the pre-war days, and no one would suggest that Great Britain at that time had negligible scientific research activities.
There is another comparison I think is interesting. While all countries have increased greatly their expenditures since 1939, the research expenditures of the Canadian government today for peacetime purposes are, on a per capita basis, of the same order of magnitude as the comparable expenditures in the United States and the United Kingdom. All of this, I think, indicates the Canadian government has not been negligent in supporting sound research and in building up national research facilities and resources. Certainly in the over-all picture Canada's relative position in research is far different from what it was during the 1930's. I think, therefore that, when listening to speeches which purport to show the lack of Canadian relative efforts in the field of research, we must be careful to inquire whether we are discussing the conditions as they were in pre-war days or as they are today. While we are on this point I should like to emphasize that, since the end of world war II, the progress in research in Canada has been even greater than it was during the war, so that one may even be talking about conditions as they were in 1946 and still be drawing erroneous conclusions as to what the 1954 conditions are.
I should like also to emphasize that research is not a static thing. It is continually changing to meet changing conditions and also, like an organism, must grow from small beginnings. The development of research is not merely a matter of money. Money will not buy trained men if they are not available, so that in looking at and assessing the growth and development of research in any country, one must always keep in mind that it is a changing picture and that it is often impossible to provide at any moment everything that may be desirable.
I do not think there is any room for complacency in this particular field. As I have said, it is a rapidly moving one, and no sensible person would dogmatically claim that at any time, in any country, at any place there is in existence a universally acceptable and permanently best arrangement of research facilities. On the other hand, I do feel that the advances made in Canada over the past twenty years have been


absolutely first-rate. I think the research council has done an extraordinarily good job and when I talk to people in other countries of the world, as I often do, I hear nothing but commendation for the work of that body. I have heard many say how much they wish their own national organizations were more similar to ours. The credit for all of this does not rest with any one government, any one individual, or any one institution; support has come from all parts of the country, from industry, governments, universities, and provincial institutions. But I do claim that this government merits a fair show of credit for guiding affairs during the period of the greatest growth and development.
I should like at this time and in passing to pay my personal tribute to the members of the honorary council. These gentlemen receive very little public recognition, yet over the years successive councils have rendered outstanding and unselfish service to this country. These men bring freely to the council deliberations their talents, experience and achievements that could not be purchased by money. They come to Ottawa three or four times a year and devote many days of hard work to the business of the council. They are men eminent in their fields, such as university presidents, deans, professors, industrialists, engineers and labour leaders. Not only can they speak with authority on professional questions but they bring to the council as well the viewpoints of the different parts of the country, and they receive no monetary remuneration at all. I think these gentlemen deserve the gratitude of this house and of our country.
I have been dealing with a few of the broader aspects of industrial research and have submitted certain generalizations. I should now like to take a few minutes to indicate how these general considerations have influenced government programs and decisions. As I have said, owing to conditions which I suggest were perfectly normal at that time, there was no appreciable growth of industrial research laboratories in Canada following world war I. The government of that day and successive governments, realizing the need for research, set about doing something which time has proven to be very wise. Without laboratories and without scientific staffs, the first national research council embarked after 1918 upon a program of scholarships to trained research personnel, and grants-in-aid to research which enabled universities across Canada to provide facilities for research. This program naturally was small at the start as there were few scholars applying, and the facilities in our graduate schools

were limited. However, this program has gone on and on, increasing in size and effectiveness, since that time, and it was perhaps the major factor in making possible our scientific effort in world war II. In 1939-40 when the great need and demand for military research became apparent, we in Canada were able to organize for the first time a sizeable corps of competent research people, and we had also a large national research laboratory which enabled the research council to provide working facilities for a staff of several thousand which they were able to recruit. Had such trained people and government facilities not been available, Canada would have played little part in military research during world war II.
But great as was the significance in war, the results of those long-term preparations are even more significant today in our peaceful pursuits. We now see in Canada a great surge of industrial research activity, not only in our government laboratories but in our private industries and in our universities. Such developments take time, and ours has followed a slightly different course from that followed in the United Kingdom and the United States.
The strength of a modern industrial nation is dependent on the quality, quantity and vigour of its applied research rather than on any detailed organization chart and, as I have suggested, it is not really useful to compare the general research organizational plane of any one country at any one time with that of another. We should rather consider our ultimate objectives, what progress we are making, and what the picture will look like in 10 or 15 years.
I think that Canada has probably made greater relative progress than has any other country in the last 10 years. I think our scientific and industrial research output is comparable, on a population basis, to that of other leading industrial trading nations. I have no desire to be complacent about the present situation, but I think we are heading in the right way, and I think we are making rather unusual progress.
I should like to say something about the way the national research council operates in fulfilling its responsibilities. As I have said, the national research council for the past 25 years has been awarding scholarships to assist in the training of scientists and has been making grants-in-aid to provide physical facilities. This program has expanded, and today between $1 million and $2 million are being spent, as compared with something less than $100,000 in 1939. My information, and I think it is reliable, is that the honorary council, who recommend all such scholarships 83276-293
Research Council Act
and awards, would unanimously subscribe to the principle that no brilliant young student should be prevented from receiving training by lack of scholarships or grants. The national research council, as you know, also operates extensive laboratories, and these laboratories were designed not to duplicate or overlap other facilities but to provide facilities in fields which were not covered in any other place in Canada, and which were needed badly. No doubt you are familiar with the general work of the divisions of applied chemistry, applied biology, radio and engineering, physics, mechanical engineering, building research and so forth.
Most of the council's laboratories are in Ottawa and vicinity. While some might argue for the decentralization of all laboratories, I think it will be found that in those countries where extreme decentralization has either been inherited or superimposed for political reasons there are serious disadvantages. The centralization of facilities makes for greater efficiency and reduces costs, and does, in my opinion, carry no disadvantage to any other part of the country. This policy, however, does not mean that where certain areas have a peculiar interest in certain aspects laboratories dealing with those projects should not be located regionally. The council therefore has a regional laboratory in Saskatoon, in the middle of the prairie provinces, which works on the utilization of farm crops and allied problems. Again, in Nova Scotia there is another regional laboratory which has been set up to deal with some of the problems that are peculiar to the maritime provinces.
I come now to the manner in which the council serves individuals and private industries. You will recall that the organization of the former department of reconstruction made provisions for setting up a research and development division in an attempt to bring the benefits of scientific and industrial research to those smaller industries which could not afford to set up their own research laboratories. We worked out a service called the technical information service and placed, in the various provinces, field men whose duties were to visit and call on all industries in their respective areas and to assist with the problems they had and give what aid we could. The research council, with its extensive headquarters information and library services, undertook the administration of this service. Over the years literally thousands of reports have been made, advice has been given, and help offered. There is no doubt that such service is of great benefit to industry.
As experience was gained, the national research council felt that this "grass roots"

Research Council Act
work, where individuals were approaching local industrial companies, could be better done by people with local associations than by employees of a federal department. Again, provincial research councils in most provinces were also supporting work of this nature, and friendly discussions between the national and provincial bodies resulted in the suggestion that it would be more effective if the provincial bodies employed all field workers, who would be provincial employees but who would have available to them the library and consulting services that exist at the headquarters' library in Ottawa.
The national research council also offered to make grants to the provincial bodies to cover the expense of such professional officers. I am happy to say that the movement has grown, and today this system is operating in most of the provinces from British Columbia to Nova Scotia. This system makes available to small industries and large industries as well the help, advice and experience of council and all other scientific laboratories in Canada. It is a service that is effective and widely used.
The research council has also organized many associate research committees. These committees are set up to support and deal with research problems that are of interest to many industries. Corrosion is an excellent example of a problem which is basic to most industrial and other activities. On such committees, and there are many, will be found research directors and technical officers of industries, universities and government departments, all of whom are intimately associated with the activities of industries throughout the dominion. From time to time suggestions are made that we in Canada should follow what is called the research association scheme which has been reasonably satisfactory in England. Research council officers have visited England many times to investigate this system, and while most officers at first felt such a system might work well in Canada, all responsible authorities came eventually to the same conclusion, that such research associations, while workable in England, are, except in certain fields, not suitable to the present Canadian situation, and for a different set of reasons the same conclusion has been reached in the United States.
There would, of course, seem to be obvious advantages in bringing together many industries in the same field for the purpose of research and development. In Canada there is one excellent example of such an association, namely, the pulp and paper association, which is supported jointly by industry,

McGill University and the dominion government. The results in this case, I think everyone agrees, are excellent, but it has been almost impossible to extend this type of co-operation through other groups in Canada. I am not going to take up more time on this point, but I should like to say that while this scheme of co-operative research works with reasonable satisfaction in the United Kingdom it does not seem to suit the Canadian picture at the present time. On the other hand, the national research council laboratories and the laboratories of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and other federal bodies do have a very intimate and close contact with individual industries which I think is an advantage found only in smaller countries.
The research council laboratories are visited daily by technical engineers and scientific officers from industry, and our national research council experts are willing and anxious to visit industries for the purpose of conferring and consulting on problems and giving expert advice whenever it is wanted. The national research council also undertakes, by contract, work for private industries, and over the years many profitable co-operative ventures have been completed.
All in all our government laboratories are far more closely in contact with the industries of the country than a superficial examination of organization charts would indicate. The national research council is not a bureaucratic institution interested only in its own laboratories and its affairs in Ottawa. It has most intimate contacts with bodies all over the country. It supports financially the provincial research councils and universities. It gives service to private industry and undertakes work when requested.
The honorary council which directs the over-all policy is made up of 18 men who reflect comprehensively the over-all problems in various regions of Canada. To illustrate: On the present council we have the directors of two of the provincial research councils, and in that way the research council is intimately acquainted with the problems of these local bodies. We also have one of Canada's leading industrialists who takes an active part in the deliberations and presents the needs and responsibilities of industry. As well, there are university presidents, deans and other scientists.
I have indicated that in pre-war days there was not very much research activity in industry. That is far from the truth today. As a result of the developments I have indicated, many industries in Canada have established research laboratories since 1939, and in many

cases staffs for those laboratories have been recruited from government laboratories.
A large part of the research that made possible the building of the plant of the Polymer Corporation was carried out in the national research laboratories. Today Polymer has its own laboratories, at Sarnia, built for its own particular purposes. We all know that applied research is one of the basic strengths of that company, and that research is responsible for the fact that Polymer has had its best year during the period when the cost of natural rubber has been abnormally low. The Polymer Corporation does not regard research as something that should be carried out in good years and cut back in poor years, but rather as essential if Polymer is to hold its place in a highly competitive industry.
The atomic energy plant at Chalk River is essentially a research laboratory, the work being entirely devoted to solving the problems of peace. The success of the Canadian aircraft industry is also based on its own applied research.
Today the position as far as industrial research laboratories are concerned is very different from the situation, say, in 1939. We have every confidence that in the next five or ten years the facilities for scientific and industrial research will build up gradually and continue to build up to a point where they will be comparable to similar facilities in other countries.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that while we do not feel that research development in Canada has reached its final and permanent form, we do feel that progress is being made in the only way in which sound scientific progress can be made. We feel that the government research organizations are co-operating with industry as effectively as research laboratories are cooperating in other parts of the world. We feel that any suggestion that our facilities should be broken up and distributed to other parts of the country is neither based on an intimate knowledge of our existing conditions, nor would it be supported by knowledgeable scientists and experts.
I have dealt with this subject in some detail, but it seems to me that, as we are amending an act under which one of the most important scientific bodies in Canada operates, it is appropriate that we should take an over-all look at the way scientific and industrial research has developed in Canada, and consider in general terms any suggestions for its improvement.

I would also like to thank the members of parliament who have served on past committees to review the activities of the national research council and the atomic energy establishment. While we naturally may disagree on details, I think it is to the credit of this house that the important activities of scientific and industrial research, so basic to our national well-being, have never been viewed on a narrow or party basis, but rather on broad national grounds.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for what the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said when he opened this discussion and mentioned that there was great interest in this particular subject. First I should like to say that I would be most ungrateful if I did not express my personal thanks and gratitude to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) for his courtesy and consideration in having this matter brought up at a time convenient to me.
In rising to speak to Bill No. 375, to amend the Research Council Act, I propose to submit an amendment. For this I offer no apology because, beneficial and necessary as this proposed bill may be, it comes as a pitiful effort by this or any other government to answer the crying need for action in order to accelerate research in this country.
I should like to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it has been my good fortune to serve on a committee of our party dealing with resources and development which was under the chairmanship of our late distinguished member, Rodney Adamson, who then represented York West. In whatever contribution I make to this debate I should like to pay tribute to him for the part he has played in what I have to say.
At the outset of this session of parliament, almost six months ago, there was a resolution placed on the order paper recommending the establishment of an all-party committee of members to study the question of research in Canada and report what action, if any, should be taken to accelerate activities in this field.
The restriction on time allotted for consideration of private members' resolutions effectively excluded the opportunity for parliament to consider this important question.
While I have no desire to obstruct proposed amendments to the Research Council Act, and on the contrary welcome even this minor and belated recognition of the importance of this question by the government, I avail myself of this opportunity to again place before members of the house the

suggestion that parliament establish now a committee to review research activities as now carried out in Canada, and report its findings and make suggestions to parliament.
The importance of research and the part it must play in the development of this nation is only recently becoming recognized, and is certainly more widespread throughout the country than the government seems to recognize. If there is one national function the national parliament of this nation should perform, and perform now, it is to ascertain the best means possible whereby it may facilitate achieving, in the interest of the people it was elected to represent, the advantages and opportunities the application of scientific knowledge offers in the greater utilization of our resources and assured gainful employment of our people.
Until a few years ago, scientific research in Canada was a question left almost entirely to academic institutions. Today, scientific research, and even more important its practical application in the interest of the nation and its people, is more than the concern of educational institutions, governments, industry, agriculture and labour. It constitutes the hopes and conclusions of the ordinary man in the street, in his search for a better standard of living, security of employment and greater opportunities for members of his family than he himself enjoyed. These worthy objectives constitute, if they constitute anything, the objectives of good democratic government.
The press of the country, which by and large reflects public opinion with an amazing degree of accuracy, has for some time now directed public attention to the need for accelerated research in Canada. The Hamilton Spectator, back in May 1945, commenting editorially on this question, made this very realistic observation, and I quote:
There are certain matters of first importance to the nation, theoretically known before the war, which have been demonstrated beyond all doubt during the last five years.
One of these is the fact revealed by war that unemployment can be mastered.
A second, scarcely less important, is the fact that the total output of all the labour of the country can be vastly increased and improved by the unstinted application of scientific thought and experiment. The industry and excellence of our scientists have been necessary to our salvation in war.
It is now coming to be understood that they will be no less essential to our salvation in peace.
A former minister of finance in this country, and a great Canadian who not only served his country well in the legislative field, both provincially and federally, but whose ability and foresight was equally recognized in other spheres of activity in the building of this nation, the Hon. C. A. Dunning, recognized, and so stated in this
Research Council Act
House of Commons, the importance of research as a means of expanding our markets, both at home and abroad. In his budget message to the nation, delivered to this parliament on April 25, 1939, Mr. Dunning said, and again 1 quote:
Can we not, In other fields, manufacturing, merchandising, transport and the service industries, apply new methods and modernize equipment in order to reduce costs, lower prices and thereby expand our markets both at home and abroad?
Cannot we adopt new ideas developed during recent years in other countries, without waiting for branch plants or refugees with capital to bring them to us?
Have our other industries explored at all fully the possibilities of research which have proved such a profitable investment in the nickel and the chemical industries?
Have we fully explored the possibilities of processing our raw materials before exporting them?
Have we sought out all the opportunities for the profitable investment of capital in new industries, particularly small industries?
These are vital questions, Mr. Speaker, for Canada's future.
Today, Mr. Speaker, fifteen years later, those questions are just as vital for Canada's future. Mr. Dunning, when he made that warning to this parliament, and through it to the nation, and speaking as the fiscal director of . the economy of the country, frankly admitted that he did not know all the answers. Nor do I, Mr. Speaker, as an ordinary member of this parliament, striving in my humble way to best serve the people I have the honour to represent.
However, I sincerely believe that in the best interest of this nation and its future, the responsibility rests, not alone on the government of the day, but on that greater authority, parliament itself, to undertake now a thorough study and review of the possibilities and opportunities accelerated research and its intelligent widespread application affords this nation at this very time in our economic development.
I am confident that no responsible person representing any branch of government, or any segment of our economy, whether educational, industrial, labour or agriculture, professes to know the answer any more than the Hon. Mr. Dunning did fifteen years ago.
We do know, however, from experience over the past fifteen years, the almost unbelievable accomplishments achieved under the impetus of war.
Surely, in the light of this experience, and facing as we are today serious problems arising from lost export markets and increased competition from abroad in our domestic markets, swelling rolls of unemployment, which this past winter reached their post-war peak, and the vital necessity of maintaining a high level of economic activity if we are to carry the heavy load of taxation

Research Council Act
which defence and necessary social services make mandatory-this parliament is warranted, if not obligated, to authorize a committee of its members to study in co-operation with the best minds that industry, agriculture, labour and educational institutions can provide, the advisability of accelerated research and its application in the Canadian economy and recommend to this parliament at its next session how this can best be accomplished.
When one considers the lack of initiative by the government on the question of research in relation to the tempo of development of this nation, several questions come to mind that should be a matter of concern to this parliament:
1.	Are we doing enough in the way of research in this country, in view of the vast and varied natural resources now known to exist in commercial quantities in Canada?
2.	Are our universities in a position to continue to provide the trained scientific minds and undertake the fundamental research necessary to assure the continued development and productive expansion of this country?
3.	Would accelerated efforts in the field of industrial research, resulting in new products, new uses for old products, improved techniques that lower production costs, enhance or help us, an exporting nation in ever-increasingly competitive world markets?
4.	Are our present fiscal policies, in relation to research expenditures, adequate to induce private industry to undertake the amount of research that should be undertaken other than by government agencies, if we are to continue to enjoy a high level of capital investment so essential to high employment and general prosperity in this country?
5.	Does the government do enough in the way of agricultural, medical and other research, in fields where this can best be accomplished by the state in the common interest of all its citizens?
6.	How does the degree and extent of research in this country compare with comparable efforts in the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries with whom our primary and secondary producers must compete in export markets?
7.	Is the national research council, efficient and beneficial and all as this council is, the right type of organization to accelerate research, particularly applied research in Canada, or should there be some additional organization more representative of the different units of the Canadian economy?
These are questions of vital importance to the future economic and social welfare of
(Mr. Murphy (Lambton West).]
this nation. The most accurate information available relative to these questions should be made available to the representatives of the Canadian people, and for this reason I believe parliament should authorize a committee of its members to review all aspects of research in Canada, as now provided for, and make recommendations to parliament as to what, if anything, should be done to accelerate efforts in this regard.
In the United Kingdom there exists a continuing parliamentary and scientific committee that deals primarily with questions related to research in that nation. The membership of this committee in the United Kingdom is composed of members representative of both houses of parliament, and in addition, one representative each from recognized scientific societies, research associations and other scientific and technical bodies.
This committee meets regularly in a House of Commons committee room to discuss subjects on which there is some legislation or other parliamentary interest. In the past, this committee has studied and made recommendations on such matters as: 1. A national fuel policy; 2. scientific agriculture; 3. development of underdeveloped countries; 4. technical assistance policy; 5. scientific relations with other countries.
Over a period of years, the committee has provided the medium for a large exchange of views between scientific people and parliamentarians. In Britain, the committee on research, representative as it is of all political parties, has earned for itself a voice in public affairs and has had considerable influence on political thinking in that country.
I think the record of the scientific and parliamentary committee in the United Kingdom conclusively proves that such a medium is capable of forming a real and effective connection between scientists and parliamentarians, something which is sorely lacking in this country.
I believe that a committee of the type that exists in the United Kingdom could serve a very useful purpose in this country, particularly in view of the tremendous challenge facing not only those qualified in the field of research, but as well those Canadians who, by virtue of their vocation, assume the responsibility to assure this nation of a continuing supply of scientifically-trained personnel to develop this country.
Just recently, a leading British scientist, Sir Robert Watson-Watt, speaking to the professional institute of the public service of Canada, expressed the view that there was a very positive and definite need for better understanding between government and scientists

in Canada. This eminent British scientist, who pioneered the development of radar, no doubt speaking from years of experience in the scientific field and its application to the economic life of a country, strongly urged consideration of the establishment of a top-level council of parliamentarians and leading scientists to help guide the development of Canada's unlimited potentials.
Commenting on the need for such a committee in Canada, this scientist, who himself was once a consultant to the Department of Defence Production and other branches of the Canadian government, had this to say:
Of all the great powers Canada most needs best use of her limited numbers in developing her unlimited potentials.
As a means of achieving this objective, a council of top-rating governmental and scientific minds was suggested.	Such an
advisory council on scientific policy in Canada could advise the government on the whole civilian field of scientific endeavour, and whether or not the various spheres of research were adequate.
Scientific and industrial research, agricultural research, research on natural resources, would all be co-ordinated in this one advisory council, which is not the case in Canada today. In the United States the president just recently directed the national science foundation to survey federal research and development programs in that nation, where today that government spends over two billion dollars a year on research.
The purpose of the survey is to co-ordinate efforts in research with a view to accelerating activities in this field. In the United States the dependence upon and importance of science to maintain the military and industrial position of that nation has been realized by the government. The national science foundation in the United States was created in 1950, about the time the United Kingdom and other countries were amending their legislation regarding research, with a view of action to enhance the competitive position of their respective countries in anticipated competitive world markets.
In the words of the act, which established this national science foundation, the purpose was:
To develop and encourage the pursuit of a national policy for the promotion of basic research and education in the sciences.
Last year, the national science foundation completed plans for a survey of the nation's effort in research and development. This was motivated by the fact that preliminary surveys fairly clearly indicated that basic research, the very backbone of technological development in that country, has not been adequately supported.
Research Council Act
Surely, Mr. Speaker, when such nations as the United Kingdom and the United States, both of whom are more advanced in their stage of development than Canada, find it advisable and necessary to take governmental action to co-ordinate and accelerate research in their respective countries, we in this parliament should seriously consider the establishment of a non-partisan parliamentary committee to study research in this country and what action we also should be undertaking if we too hope to develop as a nation and continue to compete in ever-increasingly competitive world markets.
It matters not which side of the house or from what party the suggestion for a committee comes. The important question is the authorization by this parliament, now, of a committee of its members, empowered to thoroughly study all aspects of research in this country and recommend to parliament what action this nation should be undertaking at this time. When we realize what has been done elsewhere, this country can do no less.
In Canada, we have our national research council and our scientific and research branches of health and agriculture. In my opinion, these branches of government have done and are today doing excellent work in their respective fields. However, much of the time of the national research council has, for the past decade, been taken up with matters of defence, made necessary by the fact that we were, during these years, either actually at war or building up our defences against possible aggression.
Agricultural research in Canada is concerned largely with the practical problems of agriculture, and in this regard contributes greatly to this industry. Research, however, viewed as a specific program of finding wider outlets for agricultural products, is not a primary function of existing agricultural services in Canada. Agricultural research in Canada has never been designed, planned or provided for on a long-term basis, to widen the field of edible and inedible uses of agricultural products.
While the interdependence of agriculture and industry is recognized, it cannot be said this was the motivating factor in undertaking agricultural research.
As our industrialization expands, the demands for industrial raw materials expand. Much of this can come from agricultural production.
Today, research in Canada should encompass work in the field of greater uses for agricultural products. Individual farm units cannot be expected to make expenditures

Research Council Act
on research, even though they stand to benefit materially from research efforts on their behalf.
In the United States last year, research in this regard resulted in more than $1-5 billion worth of farm raw materials being purchased by chemurgic industries. Much of this was previously classed as waste material because prior to the necessary research work being undertaken we lacked the knowledge of how to utilize this waste material or other by-products.
True, this did not solve the question of surplus farm production in the United States, but it has gone a long way to provide convincing evidence that research, resulting in new uses and new crops, offers a sound approach to this problem.
The agricultural industry in this country, given the opportunity that accelerated research can surely provide, is equally competent to explore whatever agricultural frontiers appear to offer promise.
With agricultural surpluses accumulating in this country, and our export markets threatened by accumulated surplus production elsewhere, I sincerely believe it is to the advantage of the agricultural industry of this country, and through it the nation as a whole, that a committee, as proposed by this resolution and my amendment thereto, study the possibilities of research in this field.
In the field of industrial research there is much that can and should be undertaken, not under any form of state subsidy, but rather by industry itself under the inducement of revised fiscal policies designed to encourage and accelerate research as a means to assure a continuing high level of employment and capital investment in Canada.
Research is a principal factor in the discovery of new products, the production of which creates capital expenditures and employment for our people. Research creates new wealth, which in turn broadens the basis upon which to carry our heavy burden of taxation.
Research advances production techniques, which in turn result in new modern products at lower costs of production. This enhances our ability to compete with imports in our domestic markets and the products of other countries in competitive world markets.
The extent and direction of industrial research has, by its very nature, been directly related to the economic situation in this country. It was only natural that during our pioneer stage of development research efforts were largely confined to primary industries, agriculture, mining, forestry, and to a more

limited extent, fisheries. It is a natural evolution that, as this country develops, the importance of research in secondary industries should become more apparent.
In Canada, this pattern of development of research facilities has been directly affected by the large number of branch plants located in this country, who obtained their information from their parent organizations in other countries.
For years, it was a case of the parent carrying out research, leaving the Canadian subsidiary to produce the rubber stamp copies of designs perfected in the United States or the United Kingdom.
The Massey report clearly indicates the extent to which this happened, when it points out that of 12,000 patents issued in Canada in a recent year, over 11,000 of these were the work of scientists and inventors in other countries. While this report points up the need to encourage our industries to undertake greater research, adequate action has not yet been taken towards meeting this recommendation. Until the last few years, nearly everything we used in this country was designed outside of Canada, or, at best, a copy of a foreign design.
Again, this was the result of the close co-operation between many Canadian, United States and British manufacturers, and in no small degree due to the influence of American advertising contained in the multitude of American magazines distributed throughout Canada.
Today, however, we are forced to recognize a new phase in Canadian history. We are beginning to grow up in spite of ourselves. We are beginning to realize that the belief that research in Canada must, of necessity, be on an essentially low level is just not good enough.
Two world wars have contributed much to the industrialization of this nation. Under a wartime economy it was not difficult to keep our factories running, our people gainfully employed and retain our position as the fourth largest trading nation in the world.
Today, however, with war-devastated countries back on their feet and fighting for world markets, we are facing ever-increasing competition in world trade. Today, the words "Made in Canada" must be the hallmark of good value, must represent modern production designed and produced to meet the consumer demand of a modern-day world trade. We can no longer rest on our laurels or depend for our future economic welfare on a continuing high export of raw materials to sustain our economy.

Our products must be modern and of high quality. It is not good enough to say this is a challenge to labour and management to exercise restraint in wage and price demands, lest we price ourselves out of world markets. The Canadian people have achieved a standard of living that they are not prepared to sacrifice. To continue to compete in highly competitive export markets, so essential to our economy, entails a constant effort to lower costs of production.
In my opinion, this can best be achieved by governmental fiscal policies which offer inducements in the way of taxation reductions designed to encourage research in this country. To the extent that research can lower production costs, a widely recognized fact in other countries, Canadian exporters will be able to compete in highly competitive world markets.
It will also materially assist Canadian producers to compete in their domestic market against stiff competition from abroad, and is, in my view, an infinitely better solution than a return to the outmoded practice of increasing tariff barriers to world trade.
In this country, at this very moment, we are facing the danger of swelling rolls of unemployment, a vivid memory to many who lived through the early thirties. If we are to avoid widespread unemployment in this country, we must maintain our economic growth. This cannot be done by exporting raw materials alone in their raw, unprocessed state.
Even now, lucrative, but in the long run costly as this policy has been, the end of the seller's market is in sight. Stockpiles of essential and strategic raw materials purchased from Canada are now commencing to accumulate in importing countries. Much of these raw materials have gone to the United States, but the stability of that export outlet for many of our raw materials is now in question.
As evidence of this fact, I draw to your attention the recent recommendations of the advisory board to the United States secretary of agriculture, where they recommend the exercising of authority by the C.C.C. to accept strategic materials in return for agricultural surpluses.
If this virtual barter policy becomes operative, this will materially reduce an already declining demand for raw materials from Canada. Certainly, we cannot accept agricultural surpluses in return for strategic raw materials, when we are presently confronted with the problem of finding export markets for similar surplus production in 83276-294
Research Council Act
this country. We can hardly expect to maintain the economic growth of Canada on an already indicated decreasing demand for primary products.
The United States recognizes how essential it is to maintain economic growth in that country as a bulwark against unemployment. Accelerated research is an integral part of the solution they are presently endeavouring to work out.
In 1954, the United States proposes to spend over $4 billion on scientific and technological research, which will rapidly make many of their present industrial plants obsolete. This, in turn, will give rise to a high level of capital investment, which spells employment for their people.
We, too, are a world trading nation. Our economy is dependent, in no small degree, on our ability to compete in world markets. That competition will not be made easier by the visionary action in the field of research in the United States, with whose industrial might we must compete.
The adequacy of research carried out in Canada has been a matter of concern to provincial governments for some time. These governments are primarily interested in industrial uses of the natural resources of their respective provinces, because they are closer to the problem of improving and maintaining the living standards of their population.
The experience of the research council of Alberta clearly indicates the advantages of accelerated research. The following is a quotation from the report of the royal commission on provincial development and rehabilitation, 1944, volume I, part VII, page 10:
The scientific members of the staff of the university were constantly receiving appeals for information concerning the possibility of the development of the so-called resources, to which it was impossible to furnish definite answers. Similar appeals were coming from the government of the province. The situation became intolerable. A beginning was made by forming a "Science Association" and a survey was undertaken to determine pressing problems. This resulted in a small booklet presenting to the government 36 problems concerning natural resources, all of major importance, for which no solutions were available in the then present state of knowledge. There were problems requiring solution before industrial development could possibly be instituted, and of which the National Research Council was not cognizant. In order that systematic work could be inaugurated, the association recommended the formation of a "Provincial Research Council" whose responsibility it would be to set up co-operative research on problems of local interest and especially to urge upon the national council those of large dimensions and of more general interest.

Research Council Act
The record of development in Alberta today conclusively shows the advantage of accelerated research.
In 1943, the Dawson commission on development in Nova Scotia clearly recognized the need for accelerated research when it stressed the overwhelming need for more work in research, in order to keep up with the economic progress of the modern world.
This commission pointed out that before the war per capita expenditures in research in various countries were estimated as
follows:
Russia	$1.80	to	$3
United States	 2.40
Great Britain	70
Canada	25
Again, as in Alberta, the Nova Scotia report strongly indicated the need for accelerated research.
In his brief to the Massey commission on research, Dr. J. W. T. Spinks of the University of Saskatchewan said:
It is necessary to look ahead to the time when we shall be compelled to do more of our own research to keep up with developments in the industrial field. The importation of scientific ideas is bad for the intellectual development of a country-particularly when coupled with the export of scientific brains. In time of war it leaves the country in an extremely vulnerable position. In time of peace it weakens its competitive position with other nations. Today, research has a profound influence on our national welfare and security.
I draw these expressed opinions of experts from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Nova Scotia, on the importance of accelerated research, to the attention of this house with the question: Is it not time that a committee of this parliament was set up to review the possibilities of accelerated research in this country?
In suggesting a parliamentary committee to review research in Canada and recommend what action, if any, should be taken to co-ordinate and accelerate activities in this field, I recognize the progress already accomplished.
Achievements in the field of medical, agricultural, fundamental and, to a more limited degree, industrial research, warrant a justifiable feeling of pride in a nation as young as Canada.
Marquis wheat, insulin, and the cobalt bomb are but a few examples.
During the war years, Canadian scientists, in co-operation with government and industry, devised ways and means to provide substitute products or alternative sources of supply for raw materials essential to a successful prosecution of the war.
The great Polymer Corporation in my own constituency is a case in point, as was pointed

out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I wish to reiterate what he emphasized and to quote from the report of that great industry. Its last annual report includes this particular statement:
The research that Polymer has carried out to date has not only increased our revenue but has also enhanced our position in the rubber industry throughout the world. It is our firm belief that industry should not depend on public institutions for its research work. Research, when properly directed, pays handsomely. The expansion of industrial research in Canada is a necessity if we are to keep pace with other countries and utilize our natural resources to the full.
That view on this important question, Mr. Speaker, is from the annual report of one of the government's own corporations.
The production of liquid sulphur dioxide from smelter gases met the urgent demand from the pulp and paper industry when imports of sulphur were in short supply. This made it possible for the largest earner of foreign exchange to continue to operate at capacity when gold and U.S. dollars were so necessary to a sound Canadian economy.
But I would point out that these things were achieved under the stress of war, and at a time when urgency, in a sense, relegated costs to a matter of secondary importance.
Today, in what history may yet unfortunately record as but an interval between wars, we should be directing greater effort towards accelerated research in this nation.
Certainly this can be accomplished more efficiently and at considerably less cost in peacetime than under the urgency of war.
Certainly, as an exporting nation, facing ever-increasing competition both in our home markets and abroad, we should, as a parliament, direct greater attention to the possibilities research offers in improved techniques and lower costs of production.
The present limitations of our national effort in the field of research become only too apparent when one realizes that one single corporation on this continent, namely General Electric, provides more money for research in a year than do all branches of the government of Canada, excluding research for defence purposes.
It should also be a matter of vital concern to this parliament that other nations, anxious to enhance their position in competitive world markets, have seen fit to alter their fiscal policies to accelerate research as a means toward new and better products and reducing costs of production.
In the last British budget, presented to the parliament of that nation on the same day as the Canadian budget, the Hon. Mr. Butler,

Chancellor of the Exchequer, made this statement, which I quote from that speech as reported in the British Hansard of April 6, 1954, pages 224-225:
I now wish to end as I began with our primary need; that is to improve our competitive power. Our rate of industrial modernization is strikingly less than that of America, and it seems probable that the Germans are now moving ahead of us. We shall not long continue to compete successfully in the export field with these our principal rivals, unless our plant and equipment is completely up to date.
Again I remind this house that we in Canada are an exporting nation, dependent upon export trade for approximately one-third of our gross national income.
We, too, have to compete against the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and more recently, Japan, in competitive world markets.
The British Chancellor of the Exchequer in his budget speech, stated:
The importance of scientific research to our economy can hardly be over-estimated.
To accelerate research in the United Kingdom there was included in the budget a new system of investment allowances of 20 per cent for agricultural buildings, and plant and buildings used for scientific research. This to be in addition to the full annual depreciation allowances.
I suggest that a parliamentary committee of this house should review our present fiscal policy with regard to research, and the relationship this bears to policies in other countries with which we have to compete in world markets.
Another matter I believe warrants the establishment of a parliamentary committee to study research activities in Canada has to do with greater co-ordination of our efforts in this field. Last November the Canadian Westinghouse Company did a great public service in organizing a "Canada's Tomorrow Conference", which was held at Quebec city and attended by over 300 leaders in Canadian industry, finance, education, government and other fields. One of the speakers at that conference was Dr. R. K. Stratford, scientific adviser to Imperial Oil Limited and president of the research council of Ontario. In that speech Dr. Stratford suggested the formation of a federal research council in Canada, designed to provide closer scientific coordination between federal and provincial research groups. Dr. Stratford also recommended the establishment of a reasonable number of small research units from coast to coast, on or near the campuses of universities, as a means to assist in keeping research costs to a minimum, and at the same time place Canada in the forefront of world 83276-294J
Research Council Act
science. For these reasons among others I feel, as a Canadian, that the time has now come-if it is not past due-for this nation to grow up scientifically, at least to a degree comparable to the already established estimate of our wealth in natural resources.
The industry and ingenuity of the Canadian people is more than adequate to meet this challenge. For years our universities have been training young men and young women to fit themselves to make a material contribution in the field of research. On graduation, many of these young Canadians have found it necessary to leave this country in search of gainful employment. That exodus of Canadian brains must be stopped by giving these young Canadians an opportunity to find gainful employment in Canada and make their contribution to this, the nation of their birth.
Our industrial potential is just beginning to become apparent, but it needs encouragement; it needs inducements to nurture its growth and development. What we have done in medical research, for example, insulin and the cobalt bomb, can be done in the industrial field. What our universities are doing today, even under severe financial handicaps, must now be extended to the industrial field so as to encourage greater processing of our raw resources in this country, as a means of providing employment for our people.
To longer ignore this necessary action is to doom Canadian workers to be hewers of wood and miners of metals to be processed at higher standards of living in a foreign land.
I have sufficient confidence in our democratic system of government, and our ingrained respect for our institution called parliament, to believe that a non-partisan committee of the house, delegated by parliament to study and report upon the possibilities and need for accelerated research in this country, can and will materially benefit the welfare of every Canadian.
I suggest that the tremendous development of our natural resources in the past decade challenges parliament today to pick up the cudgels laid down by those men of vision four decades ago, when they laid the basis for research in their day and age.
For reasons which I have stated, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle):
That Bill No. 375 be not now read the second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to a special select committee representative of all parties of this house with Instructions that they have power to call witnesses and send for documents and papers for the purpose

Research Council Act
especially of more effectively providing for the promotion and acceleration of research activities in Canada.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENABLE COUNCIL TO ACQUIRE FUNDS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not come here tonight prepared to discuss the national research council, but I am very happy indeed that the minister gave such a comprehensive outline both of the genesis of the national research council and of its work. I think that it was good to have this information placed on the record tonight, and perhaps the minister took the opportunity of doing so because this bill is before us. May I say at the outset that the amendment to the motion for second reading of the bill comes, I think, at a very inopportune time. We are now approaching the end of the session. If a committee were set up it would be necessary for the officers of the national research council and the department to prepare the material and data that would have to be placed before such a committee for it to make a thorough investigation of the work of the council.
I would also say that the amendment orders that the subject matter of the bill be referred to the committee. I am in agreement with the Speaker when he said that the subject matter of the bill was fairly narrow, and I can see no good purpose in referring it to a parliamentary committee. I do think, however, that the hon. member is quite right in his plea for the appearance of the officers of the national research council before a parliamentary committee, but I suggest to him that at this stage of the session it would not be possible to make the necessary preparations and to have the kind of discussion that I think this subject warrants. Consequently I shall suggest to my colleagues that we should vote against the amendment moved by my hon. friend, although I want to make it perfectly clear that if it had been moved earlier in the session in time for the preparation of data we would have voted for it. To bring the national research council before a parliamentary committee would be a good thing not only for the council but for the members of the house.
I am one of those who appreciate the splendid work that this organization has done for Canada over the years. I do not think that the minister, the council, or, if I may say so, the government, need offer any apologies for the work of the national research council. As the minister has said tonight, when the council was set up years ago there was nothing worth while in the realm of scientific research in our country with the exception perhaps of the field of agriculture because our experimental farms, filling quite a different role and occupying

a different field from the national research council, had already laid the foundations for the remarkable agricultural development which occurred, particularly in the prairie provinces. If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to say that the west owes a very great debt of gratitude to the men who worked on our experimental farms and produced the new varieties of wheat and other grains thus enabling our western farmers, in years when the season was short and when grains were affected by various plagues such as rust, to produce a crop and therefore to get some returns for their labour.
We had then some agricultural research on the experimental farms, but the minister is quite right that during the years from the end of the first great war until the outbreak of the second great war not too much was accomplished in the realm of industrial research although there were competent people on the national research council directing its activities. I should like to mention the name of General McNaughton, who gave distinguished service, and of course his successor, Dr. C. J. Mackenzie, of whom those of us from the province of Saskatchewan are very proud because of the contribution he made not only in building up the engineering department of the provincial university but also in his position as head of the national research organization at Ottawa. He made a contribution, particularly during the war years, for which I think this country should be ever grateful. Dr. Mackenzie has now retired, although his advice is still available and will be given freely. He has been succeeded by a scientist who, I believe, will also have the confidence of the house and of the country in the person of Dr. Steacie, and I am sure he will make a worth-while contribution in the days to come.
Tonight the minister outlined something of the contribution that the research organization had made to this country, particularly since the outbreak of the second world war. Those of us who know the part that radar played in the defence of Britain during the war are aware of the tremendous contribution made by the Canadian research council in the development of that very important instrument. But radar is perhaps even more important in peacetime than in wartime because of its long-term uses. I have had the opportunity, as other hon. members probably -have, of crossing the ocean on a liner equipped with radar or, perhaps more significantly, of coming through the narrows off Vancouver island on a rainy and foggy night and being invited into the captain's quarters to see the radar in

actual operation. The feeling of confidence that instrument now gives to those who go down to the sea in ships is something that is really remarkable. Canada played a very important part in the development of that great scientific instrument.
Then, too, in the field of aeronautics the national research council has done a remarkable job. Much of the industrial development in the development of the Canadian aeroplane industry stems back to work that was done by the research council. Those of us who have been on the atomic energy committee more than once have seen the atomic pile at Chalk River and know the extent to which the young men and young women engaged there are the products of developments made effective through the activities of our universities, encouraged by the national research council. We know the contributions that have been made in that regard to the welfare of our country.
I am always happy to know that the young scientists, the products of our own universities, encouraged often by our own research council, who are engaged in the development of atomic energy, are engaged in that development not because they believe it is an instrument of war but because they believe it will be of great benefit to the people of Canada and the world in civil affairs in the future. One could go on discussing the services of the council in the field of applied physics, chemistry and so on, and refer to the fine group of young men and women who have been recruited from our Canadian universities and have been used in research in this country.
I should like to emphasize this point. If there is now considerable industrial research by private enterprise in this country, it has largely been promoted by the activities of the national research council. We must not forget, and I think the minister tonight indicated, that there was very little private industrial research before the second world war, or even during the war years when research in this country was led by this most significant national organization. The results of this research by this public organization have been available to industry, so that industry benefited from the expenditures we have authorized in this parliament. The products of industry have been improved because we, in the House of Commons and the Senate, have supplied funds for this particular purpose and have thus contributed to the development and to the profits of industry.
I want to say something to the minister that I have thought for a very long time. I believe that not only should we make available to private industry in this country the results
Research Council Act
of industrial scientific research, but we should make available those results to the consumers of this country, especially concerning the wares and articles that are offered for sale. Those of us who went over the national research council building two or three years ago will recall that we actually saw certain experiments that were made in connection with the laundering of clothes. We saw that after clothes had been washed with certain widely advertised products a certain number of times, the clothes were eaten away; they were destroyed. Why should not the consumer in Canada know that some of these widely advertised products, greatly puffed up, can cause serious damage to the articles that are used in our homes?
One such product that I remember well was advertised as "no rinsing required." If one did not rinse the clothes, one soon found there would not be very much of the clothes left to rinse. I know of other fields in which research has taken place relating to consumer products, and articles for sale in this country, the results of which should be given to the public of this country so that the public might be guided by those results. In the United States there is of course a co-operative organization-I shall not call it a private organization-headed by Professor Colston Warne of Amherst University, which publishes a monthly consumer's guide. People may read in that guide the results of research into products that are offered for sale to the public of the United States. We have not such an organization in this country. This country is not big enough to afford the facilities to do that kind of investigation. But we have a public organization in the national research council, an organization unlike anything they have in the United States and unlike anything they have in the United Kingdom. Since the public, including the consumers of Canada, are paying for the operation of this national research council, which is doing such a magnificent job for industry, let that council also do a similar job for the consumers of this country. Let the consumers know some of the results of the appraisals and investigations concerning products that are advertised from one end of this country to the other.
Then, too, the national research council has encouraged our universities in the realm of research, and has assisted the universities in educating and encouraging the young men to go into the fields of physics and chemistry, as well as many of these new fields that are associated with both physics and chemistry. This is a very valuable service to the country and to industry.
Contributing as we do to the Colombo plan, it is satisfactory to know that we have been

Research Council Act
able to help the countries which are themselves encouraging new scientific research, by inviting some of the young scientists in those countries to come to our country to study, not only in our universities but at our national research council under the Colombo plan. I was interested in hearing in the external affairs committee that we have received over 400 young students in many of these fields into Canada under the Colombo plan, most of them for our universities, but some of them have been studying physics, chemistry and so on at our national research council in the city of Ottawa. That is one of the great contributions that we can make through the Colombo plan towards improving the standard of living in those countries that are just emerging from an underprivileged condition in the world.
I am not going to go exhaustively into the council's activities. I believe that in the realm of medicine the national research council is performing a very useful service to the country, as I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) knows. I believe that could be extended. We could perhaps extend that and go into research, and not only along the lines of cancer; for there are other dread diseases into which research should be encouraged. I am not going to mention them in particular but several of them will come to the minds of many of the members as well as to mine.
In a country like ours I think there is another field to which more attention should be given than has been given in the past, and I refer to housing. When we think of the rigours of our climate, the heat in the summer and the cold in winter, we must realize that our housing is still inadequate to meet our needs. A great deal of research could be done in connection with insulation and the types of buildings best suited to our climate and so on. I repeat that much more could be done in that field. I am not unaware of the fact that something has been done, that some investigation has been carried on, but I think more could be done.
The hon. gentleman a few minutes ago referred to the utilization of waste products of all description, waste from our lumber and other mills, the utilization of poorer grades of lumber and timber. Research could be carried on in connection with these and other resources such as coal so that we might not only develop our natural resources but use them more scientifically and economically.
I do not want to speak at any greater length except to say that I believe that more and more scientific research will be relied on to develop industry and to promote the
[Mr. Coldwell.l
welfare of mankind. I think that any appropriation we make to assist the development of the national research council, to make it more efficient, to make its operations more widespread will be money well spent. We are spending a great deal of money for defence, and that is all very well under the conditions that exist in the world today. We have to spend great sums of money for defence, but I believe that if we think in terms of our domestic economy-not in a world-wide sense-what we spend on research will be in the defence of the Canadian standard of living, in the defence of Canada's welfare in the days to come. I know that I would be prepared to support a much larger appropriation for the national research council in order to encourage in every way its development and enlargement in the sphere in which it operates at the present time.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, I think the amendment moved by the hon. member is inopportune. It is too late in the session. The subject matter of the bill is too narrow to refer to a committee. But I would like to say to the minister and to the government that when parliament next meets we should have a committee again. I think it is three years-I may be wrong and it may be only two years-since we had a committee looking into the operations of the national research council. Since that time we have had a committee on atomic energy, but I would suggest to the government and to the minister that early in the next session a committee be constituted to review once again the work of the national research council. If that is done I am quite sure that when the committee comes to report its findings to the house in connection with the council we shall find, as we did before, that we have a remarkably efficient and praiseworthy organization operating in the field of scientific research on behalf of the people of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the leader of the C.C.F. has suggested that he is not ready to support this amendment because of the lateness of the session. I take objection to that. We are here to do the nation's business and, no matter how late it may be in the session, if a committee is necessary we should set it up and get the work done as it should be done.
