speechtext:
I am quite aware of that. I feel sure that we should go ahead and make preparations for that committee. The scope of this bill is quite large. I would say that the necessity for a research council is probably

more apparent to the nation today than it has been at any other time in our history. It is true, as the minister has pointed out, that the work of the research council was accelerated during the times of war. I believe the same thing could be done today.
I am one of those who did not come prepared to speak at great length on this particular subject because I felt that as the bill was a short one it would not require too much debate. However, sometimes one feels that if things are to be said there is a time when they should be said, and probably I had better say what I have in mind at this time.
There are certain aspects of our economy which should be given particular consideration in the way of research. I refer to the conservation of our soil, agriculture, mining, fisheries, forests, water conservation and many others. We are faced with the fundamental problem of the conservation of our soil. As an illustration, our research council might investigate the utilization of waste wood products in British Columbia in the conservation of the water content in our soil.
In recent years we have made great use of fertilizers and this has come about directly as a result of the work of the research council. The research council brought into being the wonderful Marquis wheat and many other rust-resistant grains.
If there was no other problem requiring the setting up of a research council or a committee, I would say that the coal problem as it affects Nova Scotia and Alberta would be sufficient to keep the research council going for a long while. In the railway and shipping committee the president of the Canadian National Railways was asked the tonnage of Alberta coal that his company expected to use. He indicated to us that this was going to drop from approximately 790,000 tons this year to approximately 400,000. The dieseliza-tion of engines on the Canadian National Railways will most likely mean that in the near future the remaining 400,000 tons will not be used.
We are going to have a tremendous coal field on our hands, not just in Alberta but also in Nova Scotia and, as was pointed out, probably in British Columbia around Nanaimo. Even with the advent of science we have not learned how to utilize these products which are left over at the present time. It is necessary that a committee be set up to study every aspect of this particular problem.
There are many different fundamental factors involved and I for one would be quite willing to stay here a few extra weeks if a committee were set up to study this problem
11, 1954	4639
Research Council Act
and do a real job in the utilization of our wastes, in connection with our conservation problems and other matters.
During the latter part of last week we had the privilege of hearing the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) indicate how necessary he found research in his own particular field. He used the example of goldfish, but I am not going to discuss that at this moment. He indicated the need for a research council to study the spawning of salmon, to aid them in getting up the higher falls, and to discover the speed of various species of fish. He indicated the particular need that such a research council would fill. Mining is a business of wasting assets today. To put it another way, and it means much more, mining wastes much of our assets today. We have so many by-products in the minerals of British Columbia and in the great fields of Ontario and Quebec and in the various provinces which we do not use. We call them waste material. If we could find a proper use for those particular wastes I am sure that we would have no difficulty in reducing the price of our commodities to the point where the public would find them much cheaper, and they would be much happier to accept them.
I would say that the value of by-products has a direct effect upon the price of the main product manufactured. In my own province we have found that the discovery of minerals is important. To illustrate the work that a research council might do I should like to read from the sixth British Columbia natural resources conference for the year 1953 on page 79, in which William H. White, associate professor of geology of the University of British Columbia, had this to say:
Another tool, long known, but only recently applied to mineral exploration, is a method of investigating the minute metal content of plants, soil, and water. Plants growing on mineral deposits, and the concealing soil in which they grow, and surface waters draining mineralized areas, may contain abnormal amounts of metals such as copper and zinc. Methods now in use will detect one part per million of copper or zinc in plants or soils, and as little as one part per billion in water. Tap-water by comparison is a concentrated solution of zinc. These methods are as yet imperfect and the interpretation of results is not well understood. In the United States geological survey the investigation of geochemical and biochemical techniques is an important project to which large funds are allotted; in Canada practically the only research of this sort is done in the department of geology and geography at the university of British Columbia.
I feel, and I am sure many hon. members must also feel, that if it is important that a province such as British Columbia should set up a research department to study the particular needs in the geological and geophysical field, then certainly we should have a

Research Council Act
national body which would do likewise. I am sure that each member of the group of which I am representative would only too heartily support the setting up of a committee at this time to determine the scope of study of this research council work.
Take the matter of forests. That field is itself of tremendous importance to Canada. Much of Canada's surface is covered by natural forest regions. During the war years we learned to make use of practically every portion of our wood products that it was possible to use. We have tried to do away with unnecessary waste. We feel that a wasted product represents a wasted dollar. Forest products are a subject that should be given every study. The price of Canada's forest products, the paper that we get from those forests and other substances that can be produced have a value related to all our forest industry. I would go so far as to say that the large paper companies, the large firms having to do with paper products, and many other industrial plants which use the industry of forestry, have done their share in trying to set up a research council and to make use of every bit of their products so that they could keep the costs down. That factor in itself is well worth recognizing.
It is not so many years ago that we did not have such a thing as the various types of plywood that we have today. We did not have the many types of nylon and other wood products that we have today. We could carry on a careful study of our forestry through a research council, and I am sure that by so doing we would soon find that we could bring our wood and wood products into a world that would soon purchase them all, and be only too happy to get them. We would not have such a thing as a product we could not sell.
If those surpluses of which we speak so frequently that we have no actual use for at the moment because we cannot find a market for them, such as wheat, were turned into another product by means of research, we might have the answer to the question of disposition of our surpluses. I do not believe that we have a surplus of wheat. It is considered as such by many in the dominion today, and as long as it is not being used, but left in the fields to spoil, it will eventually become a waste. We must guard against this waste because the world is starving today for these things. I would say that Germany illustrated during the war something that we should take a lesson from. She showed us that it is simple, if you set up a research council and use your scientific ingenuity, of which Canada has such an abundance, to make use of products. She

had no trouble turning her coal into various synthetic products when the need was there. She went ahead and set her scientists to work on this research, and they did something about it. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that if we were to set up a research council to study carefully the problems on which we feel we should spend money, if we got some of these young men and women who have marched south into the United States because they could get more there for their research work than in Canada, we would accomplish a great deal. They want to be Canadians. They have been Canadians; they are Canadians, but they are living under a strange flag. Invite them back to Canada, and let us make use of the knowledge which we imparted to them.
From time to time many of our universities indicate that the scholarships that the Canadian universities or the institutes in Canada offer are not of sufficient amount to keep these young men and women interested in the Canadian field. I am sure that if we were to make a study of the efforts of the Northwestern University, of Columbia, of Yale, or of any one of these particular institutes of learning, we would find that many of our best Canadian youth, the scientists that Canada taught and made, are there today.
Since it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I would move the adjournment of the debate.

speechtext:
I see that an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy). It reads as follows:
That Bill No. 375 be not now read the second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to a special select committee representative of all parties of this house with instructions that they have power to call witnesses and send for documents and papers for the purpose especially of more effectively providing for the promotion and acceleration of research activities in Canada.
As one reads this amendment he cannot help but remember a notice of motion which stood in the name of the hon. member in the month of January, and I now read from the order paper of Wednesday, January 13:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of setting up a special committee representative of all parties, with the power to call witnesses and send for documents and papers for the purpose of examining and reporting upon the advisability of providing inducements to promote and accelerate activities in the field of research.
Now, the hon. member should consider at this time standing order 45, which states:
Forty-eight hours notice shall be given of a motion for leave to present a bill, resolution or address, for the appointment of any committee, or for placing a question on the order paper;

Now, the hon. member probably had in mind citation 657, which states:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
I would draw the hon. member's attention to the following words:
... or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees . . .
Now that means by existing committees and I have no doubt hon. members will realize the import of those words. In 1947, when, on the second reading of a bill to amend the Canada Grain Act, it was moved by Mr. Bracken and seconded by Mr. Brooks that the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization.
Mr. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order because the standing committee on agriculture and colonization had not yet been appointed. See Journals, February 10, 1947, page 55. Now what the amendment calls for is the appointment of a special committee, and
Business of the House
it is a substantive motion which should be introduced as a distinct question after notice has been given, and I therefore rule it out for that reason.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENABLE COUNCIL TO ACQUIRE FUNDS, ETC.
speechtext: I can hear representations on this question. In the meantime my remarks may be considered. If hon. members wish me to adjourn at this moment and carry on the discussion when the debate on this bill is resumed, then I am quite prepared to do that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ENABLE COUNCIL TO ACQUIRE FUNDS, ETC.
speechtext: I would suggest that that be done, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it will save time if we adjourn now and then when the debate is resumed we will be in a much better position to present our arguments at that time.

speechtext: Tomorrow we shall take the resolution to approve the Japanese trade treaty. On Thursday and Friday we shall take estimates, Thursday beginning with the department of northern affairs. Then we shall go on to transport.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
